**Sokoban snapshot v2 and artifact promotion (2026-10-07; partial API-001 /
GAME-039 evidence):** `nw-core/src/wasm/runtime_protocol.elisa` now emits a
little-endian, field-serialized Sokoban snapshot that includes options, seed,
MT19937 state, board arrays, run state, event ordering metadata, and the
variable-length undo history. Restore allocates fresh controller/history
storage, validates payload sizes, booleans, board/phase consistency, and
backwards-replays undo records to reject invalid board writes. The contract
smoke restores a generated board after a real move, verifies state and frame,
rejects malformed history/phase data, and checks matching undo continuation.

**Stage1 wasm32 checked-growth multiplication fix (2026-10-06; verification in
progress):** The fast/medium gate exposed a real backend/runtime defect in the
selected Stage1 compiler: `llvm.umul.with.overflow.i64`, used by dynamic-array
capacity growth, was lowered by the linked LLVM wasm32 backend through an
unprovided `__multi3` import. The module could validate but failed at
instantiation. In `src/backend/codegen_container_ops.elisa`, wasm32 checked
capacity multiplication now uses native wrapping i64 multiply plus a
zero-safe unsigned divide-back overflow test; the growth helper still reports
overflow to its existing fallback/trap logic. Ordinary Elisa unsigned
multiplication remains wrapping (matching Stage0), and signed i64 multiplication
retains its separate checked wasm32 implementation. The compiler-side
`wasm_i64_multiply.elisa` regression and smoke also verify the WebAssembly i64
JavaScript ABI as an unsigned 64-bit bit pattern rather than misclassifying
`U64_MAX` as an arithmetic error.

The selected Stage1 source is commit
`541788548651d43dd466d0b5210955eb966eb18e`; the fresh O3 product is
`Elisa-compiler-port-current-5417885/bin/elisac-stage1`, SHA-256
`e04b7a2213d1a29148f708468152b1087bd84aca2d9183df1818b18a12c301ab`, with
current provenance and source-tree SHA-256
`cdece4a97b0ee3fcb9de71a12cdee48a6d7be2d5b54d6ce9dd305b7960becc18`.
Focused validation passes: `match_expr_smoke.sh`, `match_exhaustive_smoke.sh`,
`wasm_integer_width_smoke.sh` (four validated, instantiated modules with no
unexpected imports), and `wasm32_darray_abi_smoke.sh` (Stage0 and Stage1 both
return 292; Stage1 module instantiates and executes). Shell syntax and compiler
`git diff --check` pass. The integrated `nw-core/scripts/gate.sh` rerun is
still in progress; its first pass over `marble_physics_manifest_test.py`
found that the on-disk `nwcore.wasm` hash is
`a7bcbe802b4bdfdb451fb9cb9f0e918758e0c6211a32e391b895e50bf633bcd4`, while
the manifest's promoted artifact expects `5f68a389c2b914ff8c6c17a6d824f1375dba12dfd21a7ab7815204c0e667f7a6`.
Do not claim a clean integrated gate or update the manifest to the new hash
until the exact current Stage1 candidate and its artifact/replay evidence have
been verified. No production WASM promotion is claimed by this compiler fix.

**Stage1 named enum-payload parity correction (2026-10-06; compiler-only):**
Fixed the two remaining enum-related failures in the 745-case
`diagnostics_smoke.sh` suite in the selected Elisa-compiler worktree. In
`src/parser/parser_types_enum.elisa::parse_enum_payload_fields`, a field-name
token local had the same identifier as its parser-machine state payload. The
arm-local shadowed the payload transferred to the next state; Stage1 therefore
recorded token index zero for named fields (for example, `"enum"` or `"affine"`)
instead of `"x"`, `"h"`, or `"n"`. The parser now transfers a numeric token
index under a distinct local name and resolves the source-backed name when the
field is committed. This preserves positional empty labels and the optional
`name?: Type` spelling; no semantic-checker workaround was added.

Rebuilt the O3 Stage1 product from the selected Stage0 compiler at Elisa-core
commit `f84b9c1034f708f69d048bd6cafb813e88c8210f`, with the compiler source at
`541788548651d43dd466d0b5210955eb966eb18e`. At verification time those selected
worktrees were respectively four and eight commits ahead of their fetched
`origin/main` refs (`370110bc2913831f59fc190f266491efcf3ccabe` and
`72a752820ab581d46bb17b3fb7158ba3879a16e3`); this records the exact current
local compiler sources used, without claiming a release tag. Stage1 provenance
is current: source-tree SHA-256
`2a70dcd5659afc5796fa3349cabdde7850a50e481e2e827b528637098ec0a72d`, product
SHA-256 `749edb6c72c0ce7dd5934c5bdb3dc6daa5691e05d859f912a0966e52b420dfd5`.
The full diagnostics suite passes 745/745, including both positive and
negative duplicate-field fixtures and the affine positional-constructor case
whose diagnostic now names `Box.Tagged.h`. `enum_constructor_smoke.sh`,
`payload_enum_constructor_smoke.sh`, and `enum_reference_payload_smoke.sh`
also pass; the last includes O0/O2 native and wasm32 LLVM verification. This is
a compiler-only correction: no port WASM was rebuilt or promoted, and the
current deployed artifact remains the hash-qualified `nwcore.wasm` below.

**Common WASM lifecycle fail-fast validation (2026-10-06; shell contract):**
The browser's `REQUIRED_CORE_EXPORTS` startup guard now requires all common
API-v1 lifecycle operations, including `nw_api_v1_drain_effects`,
`nw_api_v1_snapshot`, and `nw_api_v1_restore`, in addition to create,
dispatch, advance, read-state, render, and destroy. Previously those three
exports could be missing while the shell accepted a core reporting ABI v1;
the failure would surface later at a call site instead of at startup. The new
`nw-core/test/runtime_protocol_shell_contract_test.mjs` asserts the complete
lifecycle list and ABI-version check, and is registered in the fast gate.
Focused validation passes: this shell-contract test, the deployed-artifact
`runtime_protocol_v1_smoke.mjs` (including snapshots and explicit unsupported
cases), and `git diff --check`. The fast/medium gate was also started. The new
shell contract passed in-gate, but `runtime_include_provenance_test.py` failed:
its repository-wide scan found all 366 external runtime includes resolving
through `Elisa-compiler-latest` or unresolved `@ELISA_STAGE1_ROOT@` markers
instead of the selected `Elisa-compiler-port-current-5417885` root. This is a
real compiler/runtime provenance gap to resolve; do not weaken the assertion
or describe the fast gate as green. The subsequent two-stage differential run
recorded 93 passing Stage0 suites, then was cancelled before Stage1 results;
the overall gate therefore remains incomplete. This lifecycle guard is not
proof of full protocol support: task capabilities, effects production,
cross-build snapshot formats, and native/SDL adapters remain open under

**Current deployed Stage1 and Marble hole/wall checkpoint (2026-10-06):** The
Marble Maze hole/wall visual-overlap fix is now widened from 3.0 mm to a
minimum 6.0 mm geometric clearance for every pit, home opening, and visible
home-cup collar against every transported wall rectangle. The matching
original Python generator, Elisa implementation, browser corridor labels, and
renderer collar use the same rule. To preserve the required layouts at the

**Compiler-lowering feasibility probe:** tested a new systematic alternative
to the rejected local FMA patches using tiny residual/cone expressions in
`/tmp/nw-fma-lowering.KGAqAJ/probe.c`. Emscripten `-O2
-ffp-contract=on -S -emit-llvm` retains `llvm.fmuladd.f64`, whereas `fast`
uses ordinary `fmul/fadd/fsub contract` operations. However, blindly
replacing every `fmuladd` with mandatory `fma` would preserve the wrong
grouping for the observed native cone expression. For
`uu + alpha*(2*uv + alpha*vv)`, the `on` IR first rounds `alpha*vv`, then
fuses `2*uv` with that value. Native arm64 `clang -O2 -ffp-contract=fast`
instead computes `uv+uv`, then fuses `alpha*vv` with it, then fuses the outer
multiply/add. The native `on` assembly matches the different `on` grouping.
Thus a global `fmuladd` renaming pass is not a source-wheel parity solution;
do not ship it or equate contraction modes. The probe changes no production
sources/artifacts. Its emitted `on.ll`, `fast.ll`, `native-on.s`, and
`native-fast.s` retain the exact evidence. Any systematic lowering approach
must reproduce original native operation selection, including which product
is fused when an addition has two multiply operands.

checkout, together with recursive registration of named tuple types nested in
container annotations. In

wrappers to forward nullable strings through `sview` without misclassifying
them as raw byte pointers. The distinct safety rule remains intact: nullable

scan requires a terminated string. In

through nested tuple/container/index/unary/parenthesized forms so backend
lowering can resolve named tuple elements in darray literals.

`c27443bf9bd32f9ff7bf5081831181036ef09266` is the compiler HEAD and matches

Two genuine Stage1 compiler defects found while implementing this plan are
fixed in compiler source and have focused regressions:

1. A value-producing `match` arm whose final statement was an `if` emitted
   control flow without storing either branch value into the match result
   slot. At optimization levels this became an uninitialized/`undef` result.
   `src/backend/codegen_condition.elisa` now recursively lowers final `if`
   statements through the same result-slot path as ordinary final
   expressions, including nested final `if`s. The permanent reproducer is
   `Elisa-compiler/test/repro/match_arm_final_if.elisa`; it now returns the
   same value at `-O0`, `-O2`, and `-O3`, and
   `test/parity/opt_pipeline_smoke.sh` passes all 171 fixtures.
2. A malformed extern return header such as `-> &?` was retained as a
   void-looking declaration and later trapped inside LLVM's ABI layout code.
   `src/parser/parser_export_surface.elisa` now diagnoses the missing return
   head and skips the malformed declaration safely. The named
   `malformed_extern_pointer_return` regression is in
   `test/breadth/malformed_input_fuzz.py`; the regression-only malformed
   sweep passes 11/11 with no abnormal exit or invalid IR.
3. A non-constant address-of initializer for a mutable global reference was
   silently emitted as LLVM null by Stage1, while Stage0 rejects it. The
   backend now declines that module and reports the affected global rather
   than producing a semantically different object. The regression is
   `test/parity/global_ref_initializer_reject_smoke.sh`; it verifies rejection
   and absence of an object from both compilers. It passes on the fresh product
   identified in the 2026-09-23 checkpoint above.
4. A signed floating-point initializer for a mutable global previously
   defaulted to zero. Commit `41b6b778` preserves the sign and passes the
   Stage0/Stage1 backend native differential, including the negative-float
   case. A subsequent, still-unverified working-tree change extends this to
   constant arithmetic initializers; it is not yet part of the promoted
   product.

## Port-scope decision: N-Back is 3D-only (2026-09-16)

The port includes one N-Back experience: the original 3D face-pattern/cube
task. The reference catalog's stable identity remains `nback` so that the
reviewed fixture can still be compared with the frozen original catalog, but
the port-facing label and implementation scope are **3D N-Back** only.

The port must not implement, expose, delegate, or count as incomplete work any
of the other N-Back variants: ordinary dual/position/color modes, audio or
combination modes, arithmetic mode, variable-N mode, Jaeggi/clinical modes,
or the generic N-Back preview/session paths. Those remain available only in
the original application. Shared source helpers may stay in the repository
only when they are required by the 3D task or by source-parity tests; their
presence is not permission to expose another N-Back mode through a port shell.

Every future N-Back test, menu entry, export, option, and acceptance claim
must state that it exercises the 3D mode. The catalog audit should retain the
original `nback` row as reference data while separately validating the
port-scoped label/capability (`3D N-Back`).

## Production-shell boundary correction (2026-09-17)

The 3D-only rule applies to every production host surface, not only to the
browser's visible task hub. The browser no longer contains the generic Mode
button, generic menu screen, generic session preview, or a generic `C` route.
`C` is accepted only where a task has a real ported options surface (currently
Marble Maze); it is a no-op for the other task screens rather than a delegated
escape hatch into an unported configuration path.

The Python and SDL shells remain deliberately scoped rather than mirroring the
whole browser registry. They do not advertise, preview, delegate, or count any
generic N-Back/session path. Python and SDL now each expose the source-backed
3D Maze controller through explicit create/action/state/topology/frame/destroy
boundaries, with Python's pyglet task-hub route and SDL's `--screen taskhub`
route covered by native lifecycle smokes. Both native task hubs navigate the
full reviewed category/task list and launch only implemented native controllers
(currently Sokoban and 3D Maze);
unported selections remain inert. Python's ABI still exports the title,
task-hub, task-frame, timing, and API-level entries needed by its existing
shell; generic N-Back frame/session/menu/batch exports remain absent. SDL keeps
a separate native export unit instead of the browser WASM unit because the
latter contains the wasm32 memory-size intrinsic and the full browser
controller registry.

The original catalog and generic source helpers remain available only as
reference/parity-test inputs. They are not production capabilities. The
catalog audit (`nw-core/test/catalog_audit.py`) is the enforcement point: a
future implementation may expand the native hosts only by adding an explicit
scoped capability and its tests, never by restoring a generic N-Back or
session preview route.

The catalog fixture records the stable `nback` row as a web
`stateful_controller` backed specifically by `nback3d_game.elisa`,
`scene_nback3d.elisa`, and the scoped `nw_api_v1_task_nback_3d`/N-Back 3D
metadata exports. This prevents the default stateless classification from
silently treating the task as a generic N-Back implementation. Python and
SDL3 remain explicitly `not_integrated` for N-Back; their only native task
capability is the separately scoped 3D Maze adapter.

**Generated-play driver investigation (2026-09-19):** a closed-loop test

to its starting cell; stopping as soon as the lead marble enters a target cell
allows residual momentum to carry it back out. The next valid driver must
brake using ordinary opposite tilt/level events, wait on measured velocity and
position, and enforce a total active-time bound. The experiment made no
production physics or controller change; the original 36-case regression was
restored and remains green. This is now an explicit MM-003 test-driver task,

**Focused Marble correction recorded for the current refresh (2026-09-17):**
the fallback adapter's public `step(dt)` now has the same boundary as the
native `Simulation.step(dt)`: positive finite direct steps advance elapsed time
and execute exactly four equal physical substeps; the UI-owned 50 ms clamp and
60 Hz positive-remainder partition remain in `advance(dt, held)`. This avoids
silently changing deterministic replay semantics when a caller supplies a
longer direct step. The browser renderer also forwards the native draw
operation's `normal_scale` uniform instead of hard-coding unit scale. Focused

next floor-contact solve. `shells/web/marble-maze.js` now scales all four
rolling components with the same cap factor, and
`test/marble_maze_browser_test.mjs` stages a high-speed/high-spin regression.

change the official MuJoCo artifact or turn the bounded fallback into a claim

## 1. Mission and instructions for the next agent

Make the cross-platform port reproduce the original Neural Workshop as closely as the target platforms permit, including complete gameplay, configuration, generated content, timing, scoring, persistence, appearance, sound, and resource lifecycle. A task is not complete because its card opens, its title renders, or one fixed answer produces feedback.

This document is an execution plan, not authorization to publish releases, replace another agent's checkout, reset user changes, or alter the original reference application. Implement changes in the port and, where a reproducible defect requires it, the associated stage0/stage1 compilers. Keep the Python reference readable and runnable as an independent oracle. Any intentional behavior change from that reference must be recorded explicitly with its rationale and compatibility consequences.

All paths below are relative to this repository root unless prefixed by a named root. Proposed files are explicitly identified as proposed. Existing paths and symbols are navigation anchors: search their definitions again before editing because line numbers and source revisions move.

### 1.1 Read first, in order

1. This document, particularly sections 2, 4, 5, and the packet for the assigned game.
2. Any applicable `AGENTS.md` found in the active checkout and its parents.
3. `nw-core/PORTING.md`, including its later corrections to earlier diagnoses.
4. `nw-core/ARENA_THREADING.md` and `nw-core/docs/display-list.md`.
5. `nw-core/scripts/env.sh`, `check.sh`, `gate.sh`, and the relevant build script.
6. The exact original task's UI, logic, environment wrapper, options, and tests.
7. The port's task kernel, scene, exports, shell event routing, and existing tests.
8. Historical integration documents only as history: `INTEGRATION_2026-08-26.md` and `CONSOLIDATION_2026-08-26.md` are not proof of current compiler behavior.

Do not begin a second implementation of a kernel merely because the browser currently supplies fake state. Many real kernels already exist and require orchestration, export, and input integration.

### 1.2 Working discipline

- Record the starting commit and dirty status of every repository touched.
- Preserve tracked modifications and untracked sources. The planning audit found extensive existing changes; they are part of the working state.
- Resolve symlinks and record physical paths before running compiler builds.
- Pin compiler binaries, runtime objects, dependency versions, and the original revision for each comparison.
- Implement a complete vertical slice: original behavior → state → input → frame → outcome → persistence.
- Demonstrate both a successful and unsuccessful run from the actual menu using ordinary input.
- Keep behavior logic in the shared core wherever feasible; shell adapters own platform services.
- Do not use a test oracle or canned transcript as the production chess engine, question bank, or solver.
- Keep logs with exact commands, exits, case counts, seeds, and artifact hashes.
- Mark incomplete work as incomplete. A timed-out, interrupted, skipped, stale, or empty run is not green.
- At handoff, give the next agent the first unresolved issue and a command or replay that reproduces it.

## 3. Definition of a faithful port

### 3.1 Completion dimensions

Each catalog row must track these dimensions independently:

1. **Kernel:** legal operations, generators, scores, bounds, and errors match.
2. **Randomness:** same oracle seed/state and draws produce the same content and next RNG state.
3. **Controller:** real events and elapsed time produce the same phase transitions and results.
4. **Presentation:** visible state, layout, assets, colors, text, 3D transforms, and feedback match.
5. **Interaction:** keyboard, pointer, text, focus, repeat, and cancel behavior work from the live menu.
6. **Services:** required sound, datasets, engines, configuration, and persistence are integrated.
7. **Platform:** the above work on every declared supported platform.
8. **Reliability:** repeated runs, cancellations, loading failures, and resource cleanup are correct.
9. **Evidence:** reproducible passing artifacts exist for the current source/toolchain identity.

Use statuses `unassessed`, `missing`, `partial`, `verified`, and `blocked`, with a linked issue for any blocked dimension. Do not collapse these into “ported: yes”.

### 3.2 Equality policy

- Compare integers, booleans, strings, phase labels, counts, and discrete verdicts exactly.
- Compare ordered sequences exactly unless the reference explicitly makes order unobservable.
- Compare kernel floating-point bits where required and attainable with the pinned toolchain.
- For physics and graphics, declare a field-specific error budget supported by measurements.
- Never use one large global epsilon that can hide a different collision, answer, or outcome.
- Even when physical state uses tolerance, home/lost status, legal actions, scoring, and trial boundaries must agree.
- Compare decoded command records and string bytes independently of raster antialiasing.
- For screenshots, mask only identified nondeterministic regions; store masks and reasons.
- Do not normalize away omitted text, missing pieces, wrong answer choices, or an entire board.
- If an upstream bug is intentionally reproduced, attach the reproducer and reference revision.
- If the reference changes, freeze or deliberately advance the baseline; do not silently regenerate expected output.

### 3.3 Release scope

Initial complete targets: browser over HTTP, Python shell with native core, and SDL desktop. Validate browser behavior in Chromium, Firefox, and Safari/WebKit where available. Validate desktop packaging on macOS, Linux, and Windows before claiming those targets supported. Mobile/touch support is a separate compatibility extension unless the original control contract already translates directly; do not label a keyboard-only game mobile-ready.

“Perfect” is operationally: no known unexplained differences within the declared supported feature/platform matrix, plus reproducible evidence. It is not an assertion that finite tests prove all possible behavior.

## 4. Execution order and dependency graph

### Milestone M0 — truthful baseline and reliable tests

Deliver catalog audit, provenance, corrected assertion logic, isolated fixtures, and a reproducible baseline report. No gameplay rewrites are required to complete M0.

### Milestone M1 — shared live application protocol

Deliver stateful task lifecycle, semantic input, snapshots, ownership, deterministic clock/RNG, effects, and host services. Prove it on one discrete puzzle, one timed memory task, and Marble Maze.

### Milestone M2 — complete every game controller

Use the 45 packets below. Complete each through original menu → trial → real success/failure → result → replay/exit. Integrate options as part of each game, not as a later cosmetic pass.

### Milestone M3 — full application behavior

Close the selected 3D N-Back path, profile/configuration/media selection,
statistics, progress graphs, sound/assets required by that path, engine/corpus
dependencies, and persistence. Non-3D N-Back variants are explicitly outside
the port release scope.

### Milestone M4 — all renderer/platform paths

Run the same semantic replays through Python, web, SDL and every supported compiler/target combination. Close typography, images, 3D, audio timing, resize, and platform startup gaps.

### Milestone M5 — release evidence

Run clean builds, the complete fast/medium gate, required slow compiler gates, gameplay traces, resource soak tests, cross-platform smoke tests, and packaging validation. Produce a release matrix with no unexplained failures.

Dependency order: M0 precedes confidence in M1; M1 provides the protocol for M2; M2 and M3 proceed together per task family; M4 starts with M1 fixtures and continues throughout; M5 follows completed coverage. Avoid a giant rewrite that leaves every game partly integrated.

## 5. Baseline, catalog, and trace infrastructure

### 5.1 Proposed artifacts

Create these during implementation, not by assuming they already exist:

- `nw-core/docs/port-status.md`: human-readable matrix and current blockers.
- `nw-core/test/fixtures/task_catalog.json`: canonical reviewed task mapping.
- `nw-core/test/replay/`: replay schema, recorder, comparison runner, and failure minimizer.
- `nw-core/test/fixtures/replay/`: small permanent regression cases.
- `nw-core/build/verification/<run-id>/`: generated reports, source hashes, screenshots, logs.
- `nw-core/docs/compatibility-decisions.md`: deliberate deviations and upstream quirks.
- `nw-core/docs/runtime-protocol.md`: ABI, lifetimes, event order, errors.
- `nw-core/docs/compiler-issues.md`: minimal reproducer → fix → verified binary linkage.

The original `nwenv/catalog.py` is the starting task inventory. Compare it with `neural_workshop/ui/taskhub.py`, not merely the port's array. Enforce exact stable-ID coverage and reject duplicates, missing entries, or a test registry that happens to repeat the same omission.

### 5.2 Trace schema

A replay needs:

- Schema version and test ID.
- Port/reference commits plus dirty patch hashes.
- Compiler source/binary/runtime identities.
- Python version, platform, locale, dependency versions, resource manifest hash.
- Stable task ID, initial options, run seed, and complete initial RNG state when seed alone is insufficient.
- Ordered events: sequence number, logical timestamp, type, payload, and target.
- Host replies for engine/corpus/media services with request IDs and content hashes.
- Expected phase transitions, public state, outcome events, score, and persistence effects.
- Draw snapshots at named checkpoints, including command stream and screenshot where applicable.
- Numeric comparison rules per field and versioned normalization rules.
- Expected number of events, trials, service calls, and assertions.

Record semantic actions as well as raw input samples. The semantic replay proves controller behavior; the raw sample proves a shell maps actual browser/desktop input correctly. Do not bypass hit testing in all integration tests.

### 5.3 Reference recording

Import the original modules and use original UI/environment behavior where possible. The UI is authoritative for user-visible transitions, while `nwenv` provides useful deterministic actions and clocks. Compare the two when they disagree; wrappers can intentionally expose a narrower control surface.

Use original fake-clock hooks where available. Do not modify production Python to make a port result pass. Keep any instrumentation in external adapters and record the instrumentation version. Capture hidden answer state only in test artifacts, never in production rendering payloads.

Maintain explicit successful, incorrect, timeout, cancel, restart, and options-change traces. For games lacking a natural loss condition, use invalid moves, abandonment, and final score alternatives instead of inventing a loss mechanic.

### 5.4 Differential failure handling

Stop at the first differing transition. Print the preceding action, seed, options, expected state, actual state, first unequal field, and relevant frame. Minimize the action sequence while retaining the mismatch. Promote the minimized trace to a permanent regression.

Do not declare a compiler bug merely because two runs disagree. First prove identical inputs, dependency responses, compiler flags, source versions, and lifetime validity. A logic bug, ABI mismatch, or fixture race can imitate a compiler defect.

## 6. Shared runtime and ABI implementation

### 6.1 Proposed module boundaries

Prefer adding `nw-core/src/app_runtime.elisa`, `task_registry.elisa`, `input.elisa`, `effects.elisa`, and per-task controller modules under a proposed `src/controllers/`. Adapt names to existing abstractions after reading `session.elisa`, `trialphase.elisa`, `session_app.elisa`, and `screen.elisa`; do not duplicate an already suitable abstraction.

- Task kernels calculate domain behavior.
- Controllers own run state, trial state, options, RNG, and transitions.
- Scenes derive display commands from read-only presentation state.
- Export adapters validate ABI values and manage handles/buffers.
- Shells deliver input, clock ticks, fonts/assets, audio, storage, and engine replies.
- Rendering must not advance the simulation, grade answers, consume randomness, or write statistics.

### 6.2 Lifecycle contract

Design a versioned API equivalent in responsibility to:

1. Create application/task state from validated options and seed.
2. Dispatch a typed input event.
3. Advance logical time with a defined elapsed-time policy.
4. Obtain public state and available actions.
5. Produce a display frame and drain one-shot effects.
6. Save/restore a versioned snapshot where supported.
7. Destroy state and release every owned allocation.

These are responsibilities, not existing function names. Specify handle width, null/error representation, scalar types, optional values, and ownership before exporting them. Native pointers must not be assumed to have WASM32 width.

States must distinguish ready, preview/reveal, active response, feedback, summary, paused, loading, and error as needed by each task. Not every game needs every state; do not force source behavior into three generic phase numbers.

**Implemented slice (2026-09-13 through 2026-10-07, partial):** `nw-core/src/wasm/runtime_protocol.elisa` exports common WASM v1 functions for create, typed dispatch, logical/elapsed advance, public state, render, effects, snapshot/restore, and destroy. Its 64-slot registry returns opaque monotonic integer handles, retains a bounded tombstone for idempotent destroy, frees controller records, validates options and output ranges, and rejects stale handles. The browser startup guard now rejects a core missing any common lifecycle export (including effects drain and snapshot/restore) or reporting the wrong ABI version; `runtime_protocol_shell_contract_test.mjs` protects this fail-fast contract in the fast gate. Browser/WASM controllers now cover the source-backed task slices identified in the catalog; the contract and task smokes cover their current controller behavior. New Monkey Ladder v5 and 3D N-Back v4 saves use little-endian field serializers for RNG/history, controller, and protocol state; legacy same-build raw v1 remains restore-compatible. Sokoban uses a v2 little-endian field serializer for options, RNG, board, controller/protocol state, and undo history, with malformed-state rejection and equal post-restore undo continuation. New Tetris saves use a v3 little-endian field serializer for RNG, options, board/hand state, scoring, and event ordering; the former same-build raw v1 format remains restore-compatible. The common API still lacks task-neutral effect production, Python/native and SDL adapters, full text/IME ownership, and controller application/persistence for the complete source-derived option set. Marble physics and 3D drawing remain host-owned, and Marble's common render operation is explicitly unsupported.

Snapshot evidence: `runtime_protocol_v1_smoke.mjs` saves Monkey Ladder after a
live pointer event, Freeform Tetris after a real hand selection/drop, and the
port-scoped 3D N-Back during its second active stimulus. It restores each into
a fresh handle, compares public state (and task frames where applicable), and
continues both original/restored Tetris and N-Back runs through matching
post-restore actions. Tetris v3 additionally checks its exact payload size,
rejects an invalid RNG cursor and phase, and preserves event-order metadata.
For Sokoban, it snapshots a generated board after a
real move, restores to a fresh handle, compares state and frame, checks undo
continuation, and rejects mismatched payload length, invalid booleans, an
out-of-board undo record, and a pushing phase without a board. The v1 raw
payloads remain same-build only; the v2 Sokoban fields are independent of
compiler record layout and pointer width, while future-version migration is
still open. The full artifact suite passed on the promoted `nwcore.wasm`.

### 6.3 Input normalization

Represent key-down and key-up separately; carry logical key, physical code if relevant, modifiers, repeat flag, and timestamp. Maintain held keys by physical identity so releasing one of two equivalent bindings does not clear the other prematurely.

Represent pointer movement, button-down/up, wheel, drag, cancel, and normalized coordinates. For text, preserve text input and composition separately from hotkeys. A typed “c” in a word answer must not open options unless the original explicitly does so.

Each controller or scene must define semantic hit targets: cell, edge, tile, cup, choice, knob, waypoint. Replace the generic 5×5 mapping. Test inclusive/exclusive edge rules, letterboxing, and out-of-board clicks.

After Escape, blur, pointer cancel, options, or task replacement, clear or preserve held state according to the original lifecycle. Avoid stuck movement and duplicate activation from bubbling events.

### 6.4 Clock and event ordering

Specify a total event order for input and time boundaries. At identical timestamps, measure whether source input is accepted before or after timeout. Test just before, exactly at, and just after each deadline.

Separate wall-clock elapsed time, logical active time, and physics integration steps. Document pause/hidden-tab policy. Do not clamp elapsed time silently and thereby grant extra time after a stalled frame. If physics requires bounded steps, account for the remainder using the original policy.

Use deterministic clock injection for replay and host monotonic clocks for live scheduling. Audit the reference's use of wall clocks rather than assuming all source clocks are interchangeable.

### 6.5 Memory ownership

Document lifetime of state arenas, frame buffers, text pools, strings, engine instances, and host replies. A frame remains valid until its documented invalidation point, not “until the next arbitrary allocator call.”

After WASM memory growth, refresh all typed-array views. Exercise frame reads after multiple growth events. Reject invalid pointers/lengths before decoding; detect integer overflow in offset-plus-length arithmetic.

Provide idempotent disposal. New run, next trial, options reset, menu exit, failed load, and application shutdown must release old resources. Track MuJoCo model/data objects separately from JavaScript garbage collection.

### 6.6 Effects and host services

Give sound, persistence, media, and engine requests stable event IDs. Drain them once. Re-rendering the same state must not replay a sound or duplicate a stored result.

Host replies must carry the originating task/run generation so delayed responses cannot mutate a replacement task. A canceled request should become harmless even if cancellation is unavailable at the provider.

Use explicit loading/error state for required resources. Identify what is missing and offer a local recovery action. Optional cosmetic resources may degrade gracefully; required answer corpora or engines must not be silently replaced with fake content.

## 7. Per-game implementation packets

All 45 packets below are mandatory. Each packet inherits the lifecycle, resource, evidence, and platform requirements above.

For a given packet, the baseline kernel path is `nw-core/src/tasks/<kernel>.elisa` and scene path is `nw-core/src/scene_<scene>.elisa`. N-back is exceptional and uses the session modules specified in its packet. Original UI paths are under `original-neural-workshop-enhanced/neural_workshop/ui/`; original environment modules are under `original-neural-workshop-enhanced/nwenv/`.

Existing logic/scene suites are starting points, not claims of sufficient coverage. Read the matching sweep/diff files and identify omitted state transitions before extending them. Every packet requires tests at minimum, default, and maximum supported options; derive those bounds from the frozen original instead of guessing them.

lower the node count after grading, clamped to the source's maximum and the
degree-preserving mismatch floor.

## 8. Marble Maze: exhaustive fidelity workstream

Marble Maze deserves a separate workstream because it spans board generation, physics, 3D rendering, clocks, options, audio, and manually managed WASM objects. The existing implementation is useful progress, but its historical “100%” claim must be replaced by measured evidence.

### MM-001 — freeze the physics reference

- Record original Python, NumPy/MuJoCo, and renderer versions from the actual environment.
- Record the browser vendored MuJoCo JS/WASM hashes and upstream version/license.
- Confirm whether native and web engines use the same MuJoCo version and solver implementation.
- Compare generated MJCF text semantically: option defaults, integrator, timestep, gravity, solver tolerances, iteration limits, friction cone, contact dimensions, density, joints, collision masks, and explicit pairs.
- Include default values inherited from MuJoCo; matching only explicitly written XML is insufficient if versions differ.
- Define exact fields and tolerances for trajectory comparison before looking at port errors.

Acceptance: a machine-readable physics manifest explains every engine or parameter difference; no unexplained “same engine” assumption remains.

**Evidence (2026-09-15; partial acceptance):**
`nw-core/docs/marble-physics-manifest.json` records the live reference
Python/NumPy/MuJoCo/pyglet versions, browser runtime hashes, identical MuJoCo
release, and effective option read-backs. Both targets report MuJoCo 3.12.0;
the compiled models agree on integrator, cone, solver, timestep, gravity,
tolerances, iteration limits, and other recorded options. Native-versus-WASM
trajectory equality remains for MM-003.

### MM-002 — certify board transport

Existing anchors: `nw-core/src/tasks/marblemaze.elisa`, `src/wasm/wasm_exports.elisa`, `test/marble_board_abi_test.mjs`, `shells/web/marble-maze.js`.

- For every rung 1–16, compare board width/depth/height, start points, holes, home cups, wall extents, route metric, and time budget against the original.
- Use multiple seeds per rung, not only a single canonical board.
- Validate wall/hole ordering wherever it affects collision or selection.
- Test ABI capacities, negative/oversized rung inputs, malformed buffers, and integer/floating conversions.
- Confirm a high rung's many marbles/walls actually render and simulate; a decoded count is not that evidence.
- Compare initial marble positions and quaternion values after restart and new-trial dealing.
- Preserve source generation seeds: the original UI draws a fresh seed with `rng.randrange(1 << 30)`; incrementing a fixed browser seed is a different run policy.

Acceptance: identical certified boards and next RNG state across original, stage0 native, stage1 native, and both WASM builds for the recorded seed set.

**Evidence (2026-09-15; partial acceptance):** run
`node test/marble_source_reference_diff.mjs` from `nw-core/`. It compares all
serialized board fields/order after the f32 ABI conversion, then generated
MJCF, against Python `deal()` / `_mjcf()` for 80 cases (rungs 1–16 and seeds
0, 1, 17, 314159, and 1073741823); all fields and MJCF match. This matrix used
the current Stage1 artifact. The shared run-RNG progression is separately
regression-tested: run seed 17 yields board/grain pairs
`(889418965, 3.2267631084747164)` and `(785170443, 1.158501511057862)`, and
replay continues at board seed `57846291`. The decoder now rejects truncated
payloads, oversized wall/hole/start counts, non-finite float fields, invalid
boolean encodings, out-of-range dimensions, inconsistent cell geometry,
reversed/out-of-bounds walls, invalid home-cup ordering, out-of-bounds starts,
and trailing bytes before renderer/physics allocation or any count-controlled
loop; these malformed ABI regressions pass. The isolated
Stage0 artifact and the latest Stage1 WASM now also match on decoded board
fields and generated MJCF for all 80 certified rung/seed cases; exact
compiler/artifact provenance is recorded in
`nw-core/docs/marble-physics-manifest.json`. A headed DPR-2 run with
stored options `{rung:16,trials:1,adaptive:false,shadows:true,seconds:15}`
now enters the real high-rung board, renders three marbles and the full dense
wall layout, accepts a held ArrowRight input, and returns the source-shaped
live status (`inhuman — 15s`, `home 0/3`, `14s left`) with zero page errors or
console warnings. This proves the actual high-rung render/input path; it does
not replace the remaining high-rung trajectory and replay matrix.

**Additional evidence (2026-09-16):** a fresh headed browser run repeated the
real menu launch and Space-start path for every rung from 1 through 16 with
seed 17, a single non-adaptive tray, a 15-second test budget, and 120 ms of
held ArrowRight input. All 16 trays entered RUNNING on the official MuJoCo
engine, rendered the expected board dimensions, hole count, and marble count,
and exited with zero console errors, zero console warnings, and zero page
errors. The matrix includes the four-marble rung 13 and the dense 12×10 rung
16 board. See `lifecycleEvidence.headedBrowserRungMatrix` in
`nw-core/docs/marble-physics-manifest.json`; complete solved/lost trajectories
for every generated board and synchronized source/GPU pixel acceptance remain
open.

**Additional evidence (2026-09-16):** a fresh headed browser run repeated the
same real menu launch and held-input start for every board in the 80-case
transport matrix (rungs 1–16 × seeds `0`, `1`, `17`, `314159`, and
`1073741823`). Every case entered RUNNING on official MuJoCo, exposed the
decoded dimensions, hole count, and marble count, accepted 120 ms of
ArrowRight input, and finished with zero console errors, console warnings, or

### 2026-09-16 — Marble options persistence replay

The real options screen now has a headed persistence check. From a fresh
Marble route, the test changed the stored options to rung 2, eight trays,
adaptive off, shadows off, and the source-selected budget (`seconds=0`), then
applied them, reloaded the page, reopened Marble Maze, and verified the next
controller state was READY with rung 2, eight trials, board seed `889418965`,
and the rung-derived 45-second budget. The persisted record is under
`neural-workshop.marble-maze.options.v1`; this closes the tested apply/reload
path while generated-board result persistence and complete multi-trial browser
replays remain open.

### MM-003 — trajectory and collision tests

Capture per-step position, linear velocity, quaternion, angular velocity, state, associated hole, contact/impact events, home/lost counts, and elapsed time.

Cover:

- Level stationary marble and the rest threshold.
- Single tilt nudge in each direction and maximum tilt saturation.
- Opposing held directions and simultaneous axes.
- Rolling versus slipping and friction/spin damping.
- Speed-cap activation and angular-velocity scaling.
- Glancing and normal wall contacts, corners, and narrow passages.
- Ball-ball collision at rest, in motion, and during multiple simultaneous contacts.
- Marble over a hole at low/high speed.
- Partial fall followed by clearing the lip, insufficient-energy swallow, and home capture.
- Falling near explicit wall/ball contacts; verify collision-mask behavior when explicit pairs exist.
- Already home/lost objects and whether moving them off-board leaves stale solver state.
- Frame partitions at 30, 60, 120, 144 Hz plus irregular time sequences.
- Long-frame 0.05-second clamping exactly as original `ui/marblemaze.py:update` specifies.
- Very small positive dt and accumulated floating-point residue.

**Evidence (2026-09-15; controlled differential, partial acceptance):**
`node test/marble_trajectory_reference_diff.mjs` compares source
`neural_workshop.marblemaze.Simulation` under Python 3.13.12 / native MuJoCo
3.12.0 with the browser's official MuJoCo WASM 3.12.0 adapter, using the same
transported f32 board geometry, initial conditions, key/level events, and exact
per-frame time partition. It records every frame's 13 position/velocity/
quaternion/spin values per marble, rolling/falling/home/lost state, associated
hole index, roll/pitch, elapsed time, held-key remainder, struck/cupped/lost
events, and home/lost counts. All 36 scenarios and 1,932 recorded frame states
match discrete state/events exactly. Scenarios include every generated rung
(seed 17), stationary/rest clamp, all tilt directions and both tilt stops,
speed-cap plus angular-spin scaling, normal/glancing/orthogonal-corner wall
impacts, a narrow passage, resting-ball contact and a three-marble contact
chain, two-marble wall-plus-pair contact, four-marble central simultaneous
contact, slow pit loss, fast lip clearance, home capture, falling marble/wall
and falling marble/ball contacts including their combined case, terminal
home/lost parking, irregular/30/60/120/144-Hz and tiny-dt partitions, the 50 ms
source UI clamp, held-key accumulation/release, and a positive 0.5 ns frame.
The observed
maximum absolute differences were: position x/y `1.7e-14 m`, z `3.1e-16 m`;
linear velocity x/y `3.5e-14 m/s`, z `5.9e-15 m/s`; quaternion `5.2e-13`;
angular velocity `4.9e-12 rad/s`; impact signal `1.6e-14`. Enforced limits are
`1e-8 m`, `1e-8 m/s`, `1e-8` quaternion, `1e-7 rad/s`, and `1e-8` impact
signal; time, tilt, and nudge accumulator limits are `1e-10`. These are observed
results for this matrix, not a proof for untested scenes or a claim that
different frame partitions yield the same trajectory.

Two implementation mismatches were found and corrected by this oracle. The
Python source intentionally retains `marble.over` when a ball is swallowed,
whereas both browser adapters cleared it; the MuJoCo adapter now preserves that
reference. Also, the source UI steps every positive remainder from its 60 Hz
bites, while the browser adapters discarded any remainder at or below 1 ns;
both now step all positive remainders. The reference's 50 ms frame can produce
a fourth tiny floating-point bite after three nominal bites, and both adapter
regressions now assert that behavior. Broader MM-003 cases listed above remain
open; do not mark this requirement complete.

### MM-004 — lifecycle/options/scoring

Read original `_read_options`, `_reset`, `start_run`, `_next_trial`, `restart`, `_settle`, `_finish`, `score`, and `_pay_coach`.

- Implement configured initial rung, number of trials, adaptive flag, and time override.
- Preserve restart semantics: reset the physical simulation without granting a new trial budget.
- Preserve held-key fractional accumulator reset semantics on restart, blur, exit, and options.
- Record every trial result before advancing, including rung, elapsed, home, and lost counts.
- Apply adaptive progression only when enabled and at the same source lifecycle boundary.
- Match feedback duration and whether Space can skip it.
- Match key semantics exactly: Space starts from READY/DONE and may skip a
  won/lost feedback interval; Enter is not a native Marble Maze shortcut.
- Match final summary text, best rung, total seconds, home/lost totals, and result persistence.
- Audit source `score()` carefully: it counts rows with zero lost marbles as wins, which can differ from the timeout verdict. Preserve/document that observable behavior unless deliberately changed in both applications.
- Implement source coach feedback if enabled; ensure it does not expose future answers.
- Cancel pending animation/timer callbacks and stale host requests on every exit path.
- Prevent a canvas click during feedback from mutating generic `taskState` and clearing a Marble verdict.

Acceptance: replay complete runs with adaptation on/off, different trial counts, timeout override, partial success, lost marbles, restart, and final summary; compare all stored results and visible feedback.

Replace duplicated category arrays and integer dispatch trees with stable catalog IDs. Keep category/order metadata separate from IDs. Generate or validate export/test/menu mappings from the same reviewed manifest while retaining an independent comparison to the original catalog.

Use explicit task capability records: kernel/controller availability, required services, supported input, options schema, and platform status. Unsupported entries must be explained honestly during development, and none may remain unsupported at the declared full-port release.

**Implementation checkpoint (2026-09-20; partial, not closure):** the schema-v4
reviewed catalog now owns ordered category labels, task labels and positions,
and explicit port overrides. `generate_task_registry.py` deterministically
produces the browser's menu label/order and stable-ID module, which `index.html`
imports; its `--check` mode runs in the gate. The deliberate original `nback`
→ port-only `nback_3d` boundary is encoded as a manifest override. The

the selection resolver, and absence of numeric controller dispatch. Browser
contracts assert stable IDs, and the artifact gate passed after updating stale

and export mappings are not generated from this manifest; the capability

controller, kernel/scene modules, WASM lifecycle exports, and stateful web,

### APP-002 — navigation contract

Audit title shortcuts, game selection, the scoped 3D N-Back options, task
options, user selection, sound/image selection needed by included tasks,
progress graph, configuration editor, and full screen. Map every original
shortcut and visible affordance that remains in the port; do not reproduce
non-3D N-Back mode selection.

Test Escape from each nested screen, returning to the correct selection, options apply/cancel, opening a game twice, and rapid menu changes during loading. Every visible button must have a meaningful supported action.

Preserve per-task versus global settings boundaries. A task's options must not accidentally change another task's rung or a shared seed. Validate configuration before mutating live state.

and final 3D statistics. Include only the mode flags that affect the 3D task;
arithmetic, audio, combination, variable-N, and other original-only flags are
out of scope and must not appear in the port UI or ABI.

Check that a response during a blank period is handled exactly as the original does; pressing “Next” must not be a substitute for live timing. Verify pause, resume, and session abort accounting.

## 10. Production resources, audio, content, and engine services

### RES-001 — inventory and licensing

Inventory `original-neural-workshop-enhanced/res`, `data`, `Readme-resources.txt`, `requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml`, and `nw-core/res`. Record logical ID, source path, hash, size, license/attribution, optional/required status, consumers, and decode format.

Include fonts, images, marble textures, sound sets, word lists, question banks, sentence data, chess resources, and third-party WASM. Verify redistribution terms before packaging. Local availability does not imply permission to distribute.

### RES-002 — asset identity and loading

Use logical resource IDs, not paths baked into every scene. Resolve native and web URLs through a manifest. Handle case sensitivity consistently, especially Windows/macOS versus Linux.

Loading order must not alter RNG consumption or generated content. Wait for assets whose dimensions affect layout, or provide their measured dimensions as versioned metadata. Prevent stale loads from overwriting new task state.

Test corrupt files, missing required assets, missing optional variants, invalid image dimensions, interrupted loads, and offline operation where promised. The missing dark logo warning is a concrete regression case: verify fallback placement and diagnostic wording.

### RES-003 — audio

Inspect original `audio.py`, `media.py`, task sound calls, and display SOUND commands. Match selected sound identity, pitch/rate, gain, overlap, and stop/reset semantics.

In browsers, unlock audio through an ordinary user gesture and handle suspended contexts. Schedule stimuli using the task clock with measured output latency where relevant. Do not replay a sound each frame because its command remains in a display list.

Test muted mode, missing audio, rapid repeated cues, task exit mid-sound, pause/resume, and device changes. Audio-dependent gameplay cannot be declared complete using silent placeholders.

### RES-004 — corpora and external engines

For trivia/verbal/crossword/scrabble/scramble, define production provider schemas and deterministic selection rules. Freeze the corpus used for regression while allowing versioned user content. Validate empty or incompatible data.

For chess and any other external engine seam, implement a production provider with error handling, lifecycle, and compatibility tests. A recording of answers generated during testing is only a test fixture.

If an engine runs asynchronously, tag every request with task generation and position hash. Reject results for outdated positions. Match order where consumers choose the first candidate; count equality is only enough where source behavior uses counts.

Inspect original `ui/scene3d.py`, `render3d.py`, and the task-specific scene builders. Define mesh/material/camera/light/instance data and lifecycle. Decide whether to extend the shared display contract or attach a versioned 3D scene payload.

## 12. Compiler correctness and reproducibility

### COMP-001 — identify every compiler used

Read `scripts/env.sh`, `build-toolchain.sh`, `build_pymodule.sh`, each wrapper, and compiler test helpers.

Record stage0 binary, stage1 binary, driver script, runtime object/source, LLVM/clang/wasm-ld versions, target triple, optimization settings, and source hashes. Explicitly set alternate variable names such as `ELISAC` only when a called script actually uses them.

Require executable binaries and expected identities. Do not accept a helper's success exit when it prints SKIP for missing prerequisites. Compare source provenance to binary mtime/hash after compiler fixes.

### COMP-002 — numerical/language regression corpus

Preserve and extend regressions for:

- Strict FP/FMA contraction and cancellation-sensitive expressions.
- Python-compatible rounding, negative division/modulo, and signed/unsigned conversions.
- MT19937, getrandbits, randbelow, shuffle/sample, and next RNG state.
- Dict insertion ordering, set iteration where observable, and stable ties.
- Namespace-qualified constants, structs, returns, and sibling function resolution.
- String literal versus sview constructor overloads.
- Arena/region forwarding, aggregate field mutation, and returned views.
- Optional reference narrowing, pointer casts, field access, and null handling.
- Or-pattern bindings, scope shadowing, match alternatives, and loop captures.
- Large struct literals, stack usage, compiler time, and unexpected function decline.
- `@link_name` validation, emitted symbol name, native linkage, and collisions.
- WASM target predicates, allocator selection, memory growth, runtime imports, and deallocation.
- Pymodule/export ABI widths, string lifetimes, and malformed arguments.

A regression must execute and assert a result, not merely compile. Where the correct behavior is rejection, assert diagnostic category and nonzero exit on both stages.

### COMP-003 — defect workflow

1. Reproduce with fixed source/input/flags and known binary hashes.
2. Establish reference/language semantics independently; stage0 is not infallible.
3. Reduce to the smallest source with an observed wrong result or crash.
4. Save the reproducer in the actual compiler repo's test/repro or equivalent.
5. Inspect emitted IR and runtime memory when code generation is implicated.
6. Fix the narrow compiler phase responsible, including qualification/provenance metadata where necessary.
7. Add negative/nearby cases so the fix cannot merely bypass validation.
8. Run focused regression, appropriate stage suite, and affected port suites.
9. Rebuild the pin; verify the same reproducer and live port using the new binary.
10. Record source commit/dirty patch, binary hash, and result in the issue ledger.

Do not disable semantic analysis, enable relaxed FP, substitute canned answers, or change source algorithms merely to hide a compiler miscompile.

### COMP-004 — stage1 native and WASM independence

The current standard web build is stage0. Add a distinct stage1 WASM path that emits a separate object/module with attributable flags and no implicit fallback to stage0.

Compare exported names/signatures, import requirements, display bytes, action replay outcomes, and RNG states. Build a clean stage1 product and run it without stage0 available except in explicitly labeled bootstrap steps.

For self-hosting, retain gen2/gen3/gen4 identities and fixpoint evidence required by the compiler's current gate. An exit 137 is only evidence of signal termination; do not label it out-of-memory without process/system evidence. Preserve logs and mark the gate incomplete.

### COMP-005 — shared workspace isolation

Compiler sources and binaries may be used by other tasks. Create task-owned worktrees/build paths when needed, preserving user edits and disabling rebuilding git hooks for the operation. Never reset or stash another task's files as a routine integration technique.

Serialize resource-heavy compiler jobs in this task. Record external contention as context, not as proof that a failure is harmless. Avoid unlimited retries; minimize the failing case or diagnose the harness before rerunning a large suite.

## 13. Repair verification infrastructure before relying on it

### TEST-001 — correct frame assertions

In `task_game_input_smoke.mjs`, keep raw byte arrays and decoded command arrays in separate variables. Compare matching representations and use semantic expectations for visible changes.

Prove the test fails when the active frame is deliberately replaced by the ready frame, when an input is ignored, and when the game returns the wrong outcome. Do not require every action to change pixels: a legitimate blocked move may leave the same frame.

Retain title/ABI smoke coverage but rename its claims accurately. Add tests that invoke the real stateful API so externally supplied phase flags cannot manufacture a “playing” result.

### TEST-002 — harness exits and counts

In `check.sh`, capture checker exit status as well as output. Require all of: expected compiler invoked, compilation successful, link successful, execution successful, expected nonzero case count, zero mismatches.

Reject unknown suite/stage filters. Detect zero discovered tests. Treat missing dependencies and scripts as explicit skips that fail required release coverage. Have the gate fail closed if sourcing `env.sh` fails.

Store structured results rather than parsing only the last text line. Preserve stdout and stderr separately for diagnosis.

### TEST-003 — scratch directories, signals, locks

Historical scope runs lost their scratch directory, and prior narration attributed this to macOS cleanup or resource pressure without sufficient evidence. Diagnose it properly before preserving that explanation.

The scope harness currently installs the same removal trap on EXIT, INT, TERM, and HUP. A signal handler that removes the work directory but does not exit can allow the script to continue into “file not found” failures. Reproduce signal delivery in an isolated harness and verify termination behavior. This is a concrete alternative to investigate, not a proven diagnosis of the historical failures.

- Use a validated per-run temporary directory and fail immediately if creation fails.
- Clean up on EXIT; explicit signal handlers should exit with appropriate signal-derived status.
- Preserve failure artifacts when requested or move them to an evidence directory.
- Never recreate vanished intermediate state and then report the run as uninterrupted.
- Record interruption as interruption and rerun the affected complete unit.
- Test checker lock interruption, ownerless locks, PID reuse, stale owners, and concurrent process startup.
- Replace global `/tmp/nw_*_oracle.txt` files with run-local inputs, or serialize every consumer of those paths.
- Do not remove a lock owned by another live process.
- If timeouts are retried, retain both outcomes and label retries; a retry pass does not erase flaky behavior.

Acceptance: injected interruption exits promptly, no subsequent cases run from deleted state, no false PASS result appears, and concurrent runs cannot overwrite each other's artifacts.

### TEST-004 — evidence tiers

| Tier | Checks | What it proves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit/kernel | Pure operations, edge cases, randomized properties | Local algorithm behavior. |
| Differential | Same inputs against frozen original | Behavior for recorded cases. |
| Scene | Injected state to commands | Presentation mapping for those states. |
| ABI | Export types, bytes, ownership, invalid inputs | Transport and boundary behavior. |
| Controller replay | Real actions/time from initial state | Reachable lifecycle and outcome behavior. |
| End-to-end | Actual shell input and visible screenshots | User can operate the integrated game. |
| Soak | Many runs, restarts, exits, failures | Lifecycle/resource reliability. |
| Release matrix | Clean packaged builds on targets | Delivered artifact capability. |

All tiers matter; none subsumes all others. A correct title and three draw commands are not proof of a visible marble board.

## 14. Concrete validation commands and how to report them

Run commands from the repository root unless the block says otherwise. Inspect scripts first, since toolchain roots may have changed.

### 14.1 Read-only identity capture

```bash
git status --short
git rev-parse HEAD
git -C original-neural-workshop-enhanced status --short
git -C original-neural-workshop-enhanced rev-parse HEAD
readlink original-neural-workshop-enhanced
readlink stage0-elisa-compiler
readlink stage1-elisa-compiler
```

Then inspect `nw-core/toolchain/PROVENANCE` and hash the actual binaries using the platform's SHA-256 utility. Include dirty-source identity, not just branch names.

### 14.2 Pinned port builds and differential suites

The first command is only an example of a focused suite. Replace the suite name with the task/module under change. Do not run multiple full `check.sh` invocations concurrently while shared fixture paths exist.

`gate.sh` currently covers differential/WASM/compiler tiers; it does not establish every game's end-to-end playability or all platform packages. Add those missing gates.

To verify the latest locally installed Elisa Stage1 product without replacing
the port-pinned compiler or overwriting the served artifact, build into a fresh

NW_STAGE1_VERIFY_DIR="$(mktemp -d /tmp/nw-stage1-current.XXXXXX)"
ELISA_STAGE1_ROOT="/Users/torarinvikbjarko/Documents/Coding Projects/Elisa Projects/Elisa-compiler" \

At the 2026-09-15 checkpoint this emitted the same `-O2` object and WASM

In this checkout, the unoverridden `build_stage1_wasm.sh` correctly refuses

## 15. Performance, fault handling, and long-session stability

### PERF-001 — bounded resource behavior

Measure startup time, first-task latency, frame time distribution, maximum controller tick time, WASM memory, native allocations, GPU resources, and audio nodes. Record hardware/build identity and workload.

Use dense boards, top rungs, long corpus text, many objects, and repeated scene changes. Compare to the original where possible. Establish practical thresholds from measured workloads; do not introduce arbitrary universal millisecond limits.

Fix repeated allocation in rendering when it materially harms frame pacing, but preserve behavior. Do not reduce simulation accuracy or omit commands to hit a benchmark.

### PERF-002 — deterministic rendering rate tests

Render identical state 1, 10, and 100 times without advancing time. Require identical game/RNG/score state and no duplicate effects. Replay the same logical action sequence with different render frequencies.

For continuous simulations, use equal time partitions to establish differential parity first. Then assess cross-frame-rate stability as a separate property and compare source sensitivity.

### FAULT-001 — explicit failures

Inject missing engine, missing corpus, failed font/image/audio decode, WASM allocation failure where testable, storage rejection, invalid ABI input, and canceled background load.

Each case must show a recoverable UI or controlled exit, preserve completed results, and avoid misleading “game started” placeholders. Retrying a load must not duplicate subscriptions, models, or result records.

### SOAK-001 — repeated lifecycle

For each family, run at least 100 create/start/cancel/destroy cycles and a multi-session sequence. Include task switches during reveal, dragging, physics, audio, feedback, and asynchronous resource work.

Measure live objects before/after and after supported allocator cleanup. Do not confuse reserved heap capacity with leaks, but document plateau behavior and surviving allocations.

## 16. Packaging and supported-platform release work

### PKG-001 — clean source reproducibility

Build from a clean checkout with documented dependencies and no access to developer-specific absolute paths. Verify required untracked sources/assets from the development tree are included in the intended change before release.

Generate a manifest containing source identity, compiler identities, ABI version, dependency/license inventory, and artifact hashes. Compare development and packaged behavior using the same smoke replay.

### PKG-002 — browser distribution

Serve generated bindings and WASM with the correct paths and content types. Version assets so stale caches cannot mix incompatible code and module versions. Test reload after an update, missing asset errors, and Firefox/Safari.

If offline capability is promised, implement and test a complete offline resource strategy. Avoid a service worker until its update/invalidations are designed; an old cached module can make fixed source appear broken.

### PKG-003 — desktop distribution

Package native libraries, runtime resources, fonts, sound, and engines for each declared OS/architecture. Check relative resource resolution, writable profile directories, Unicode paths, and running outside the source directory.

Use OS-appropriate linking and runtime library discovery. Test launch on a machine or isolated environment without the developer toolchain. Do not use headless success as evidence of visible window behavior.

### PKG-004 — release feature matrix

For each OS/browser/architecture record all task IDs, required services, options, audio, storage, and 3D capability. An unavailable target remains explicitly unsupported until tested.

Publishing/signing/distribution are separate user-visible operations; prepare reviewable artifacts and use the session's authorization boundaries for any external release.

## 17. Work allocation and agent handoffs

### 17.1 Suggested work packages

- Foundation owner: catalog, runtime protocol, ownership, event ordering, exports.
- Verification owner: reference traces, harness reliability, case counts, mutation checks.
- Discrete puzzle owner: Sokoban, Maze, Hanoi, Sudoku, Go, N-in-a-row.
- Timed/memory owner: Monkey Ladder, Concentration, Removals, tracking/occlusion tasks.
- Language/content owner: trivia, verbal, crossword, scrabble, scramble, algebra/numberology.
- Physics/3D owner: Marble Maze, Buzz Wire, Two Hands, 3D Maze/Sokoban.
- Platform owner: renderer completeness, fonts/assets/audio/storage, native packaging.
- Compiler owner: minimal reproductions, stage parity, pin rebuilding, runtime drift.

These are work packages, not a request to create new user-visible tasks automatically. Coordinate through allowed subagent/worktree mechanisms when parallel work is used.

### 17.2 Shared-file rules

The runtime protocol, task registry, export surfaces, and build scripts have many consumers. Agree on their interfaces before parallel controller work. Give one owner responsibility for final integration of each shared file.

Keep task-local implementations and tests separate until the protocol is stable. Do not let each agent invent an incompatible state handle, time unit, string encoding, or error code.

### 17.3 Required handoff template

For every completed or interrupted package, report:

- Package/game ID and exact scope.
- Starting and ending source identities, including dirty diffs.
- Original modules and behavior traced.
- Changed files and public interface changes.
- Verified commands with exit status, cases, and artifact location.
- A successful real input replay and an unsuccessful/boundary replay.
- Known deviations and untested platforms/options.
- Resource ownership and cleanup evidence.
- Compiler fixes and actual rebuilt binary hashes, if applicable.
- The next unresolved item with a minimized reproducer.
- Whether generated artifacts/resources are included in a clean checkout.

Do not write “all tests pass” without identifying which tests. Do not present a historical pass as a pass after unrelated subsequent changes.

## 18. Acceptance checklist

### 18.1 Per-game gate

A game can be marked complete only when all applicable boxes are checked:

- [ ] Original catalog ID and menu location match.
- [ ] Every supported option is parsed, validated, applied, and persisted.
- [ ] Real generated state replaces production starter fixtures.
- [ ] Correctness is computed from that state.
- [ ] Input uses real keyboard/pointer/text semantics and hit regions.
- [ ] Time, reveal, animation, and response boundaries match the reference.
- [ ] Success and incorrect/timeout/abandon paths reach the correct terminal state.
- [ ] Feedback, score, next trial, adaptation, and summary match.
- [ ] Images/fonts/audio/corpora/engines are real and load reliably.
- [ ] Hidden state does not leak through the presentation boundary.
- [ ] Original/port replay comparison passes on both compilers where supported.
- [ ] The game is operable in the actual web, Python, and SDL shells.
- [ ] Screenshots are reviewed, including difficult/high-rung states.
- [ ] Restart, exit, options, blur, and delayed callbacks are correct.
- [ ] Result writes occur once and survive reopening.
- [ ] Disposal/soak tests show bounded live resources.
- [ ] Any deviation has an explicit compatibility decision.
- [ ] Evidence artifacts identify the current build.

### 18.2 Whole-port gate

- [ ] All 45 original catalog entries pass their per-game gate.
- [ ] Registry comparisons detect additions/removals in the original.
- [ ] No required production task uses a constant question/answer fixture.
- [ ] No generic movement counter substitutes for domain state transitions.
- [ ] Main menus, profiles, options, media selection, statistics, and graphs work.
- [ ] The scoped 3D N-back mode and its live session accounting are covered; non-3D N-back variants are explicitly excluded from the port gate.
- [ ] Stage0 and stage1 semantics/code generation are verified for the port.
- [ ] Stage1 WASM coverage is distinguished from stage0 web build coverage.
- [ ] Compiler/runtime provenance and packaging compiler provenance are complete.
- [ ] Required fast/medium/slow gates have current successful results.
- [ ] No required test is hidden behind SKIP or an ignored process exit.
- [ ] Reference scene, controller replay, and shell E2E coverage are independently present.
- [ ] Supported browser and desktop matrix is tested from clean artifacts.
- [ ] Required assets and licenses are included.
- [ ] Long-session, cancellation, failure, and resource-lifecycle checks pass.
- [ ] Release notes state any remaining intentional limitations accurately.

## 19. Risk register and stopping rules

| Risk | Observable symptom | Investigation | Closure evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fixture mistaken for game | Screen changes but challenge/answer never changes | Trace controller state and actual generator calls | Seeded live runs with distinct challenges and correct results |
| Tests approve supplied phases | “Running” passes without any live transition | Invoke actual stateful API; mutation-test ignored input | Broken transition is caught |
| Wrong compiler selected | Unexplained stage drift across identical source | Hash all executables and wrapper environment | Reproducible pinned builds |
| Dangling frame/string storage | Geometry valid, labels corrupt | Arena/pool lifetime and memory growth tests | Stable bytes after repeated allocation |
| Missing physics cleanup | Memory grows each game visit | Model/data ownership counters | Bounded live allocations |
| Time partition mismatch | Different win/loss after frame stalls | Compare ordered dt/input traces to original | Matched event/outcome trace |
| Corpus fixture in production | Same question every trial | Provider wiring and RNG draw audit | Real versioned content selection |
| Incorrect input transform | Clicked visible piece differs from selected one | DPR/letterbox/world-coordinate mapping | Edge and resize picking tests |
| Hidden callback survives exit | Old game modifies newly opened screen | Generation IDs and cancellation tests | No stale state/effect writes |
| Harness signal cleanup | Later cases lose files after interrupt | Explicit signal-injection test | Prompt interrupted exit with retained diagnostics |
| Unsupported renderer path | Titles render; objects/sounds absent | Primitive/asset command inventory | Every required command exercised visibly |
| Premature release claim | Smoke green, actual game unsolvable | Per-game completion evidence audit | All required dimensions independently verified |

Stop expanding a failing suite until the first failure is classified. If an external prerequisite is unavailable, continue independent implementation and mark only the dependent evidence blocked. Do not erase a test, weaken an assertion, or replace a behavior with a fixture to turn a dashboard green.

## 20. How to maintain this plan

Keep stable IDs when updating tasks so future agents and evidence reports can refer to them. Add dated findings to the status ledger rather than rewriting historical evidence as if it described the newest revision.

After each vertical slice, update the per-game matrix with links to source, replay, screenshots, and test reports. Track remaining gaps in controller, services, and platforms independently. If the original gains a task or changes behavior, update the catalog baseline and add explicit migration work.

The final completion statement must describe what a user can actually do in the shipped application, which platforms were tested, and any deliberate differences. The acceptance checklists above are the evidence needed to make that statement.

### 2026-09-13 — `@test` hidden-store ABI fixed; toolchain identity discrepancy recorded

This entry supersedes the earlier ledger text above that leaves the readonly
test-runner crash open. It does not close the full stage1 compiler or port plan.

#### Root cause and source change

The candidate crash was an ABI mismatch, not a failure in
`Semantic.check_readonly_refs`: a test function calling the parser or semantic
helpers was assigned a hidden packed-AST-store parameter by stage1 backend body
analysis, while the generated native C dispatch shim correctly invoked each
`@test` function with the ordinary zero-argument ABI. Stage0 treats test
functions as entry points that own their region and create a store locally.
The stage1 body later interpreted an absent register as its packed store and
faulted in `ctx_aos_store_alloc`.

In `worktrees/elisa-compiler-nw/src/backend/codegen_declare_signature.elisa`,
the declaration logic now recognizes `@test` for both intrinsic compiler-store
classification and transitive store forcing. Existing body analysis remains
responsible for discovering an AST root and initializing the local region/store.
This also makes the rule independent of a test's enclosing module name.

The native test-runner parity script now includes
`worktrees/elisa-compiler-nw/test/parity/readonly_lookup_smoke.elisa`, which
parses a source string into `Ast::File` and passes that AST through semantic
analysis. The stale open-crash statements in COMP-006/COMP-007 have been
superseded in `nw-core/docs/compiler-issues.md` and `nw-core/docs/port-status.md`.

### 2026-09-14 — qualified generic owner lookup fixed and differential crash cluster cleared

This entry records a stage1 wrong-code defect found while resuming the native
port sweeps. It closes the qualified generic resolution defect only; it does
not close the other compiler or product workstreams.

#### Root cause, implementation, and regression

The backend's `generic_index_of(generics, name)` is the intended resolver for a
bare identifier: it prefers the active module, then a top-level template, then
the first same-named template. Three `Expr.Scope` paths incorrectly reused
that name-only lookup for `Module::member`. A top-level `put[T]` could therefore
steal `Ints::put(41)`, even when `Ints::put` was an ordinary monomorphic
function. The regression returned 140 on the pre-fix stage1 candidate versus
168 on stage0. The same owner confusion explained the `pyset` failure: the
wrong `put[T]` body treated the set's darray receiver as an IndexMap and
crashed while reallocating its arena-backed storage.

The compiler source now has an exact `(owner, name)` generic lookup, a scoped
owner-path resolver for direct, aliased, and nested modules (with enclosing
module fallback only when no direct function takes precedence), and explicit
call dispatch by the resolved generic slot. Instantiation temporarily pins
the selected template owner so its existing signature/body/cache queries
cannot fall back to a same-named top-level generic; the prior owner is restored
before returning. Bare generic identifier behavior is unchanged.

The regression fixture
`worktrees/elisa-compiler-nw/test/repro/qualified_generic_scope_shadow.elisa`
checks a monomorphic member shadowed by a top-level generic, an inferred
module generic, explicit one-type application, and explicit two-type
application. The executable parity test is
`worktrees/elisa-compiler-nw/test/parity/qualified_generic_scope_smoke.sh` and
is included in `nw-core/scripts/gate.sh` as `qualified_generic_scope`.

#### Verification and exact artifact scope

- Reproduced before fix: `qualified_generic_scope_smoke.sh` using the old
  candidate with `ELISA_ALLOW_STALE_STAGE1=1` reported `stage0=168`,
  `stage1=140`, and failed as required.

- Candidate v6 passes the focused regression: stage0 and stage1 both return
