### 2026-09-14 — large aggregate `sret` optimizer blow-up fixed in isolated stage1 v12

This entry supersedes only the COMP-003 RSS status in earlier snapshots. It does
not certify every compiler path, promote the isolated compiler candidate, or
mark the cross-platform port complete.

#### Reproducer and root cause

`nw-core/test/repro/stage1_glyphs_compile_memory.elisa` imports
`src/glyphs.elisa` without calling any Glyphs routine. Before the fix, its
stage1 `-O1`/`-O2` module optimization exceeded the ordinary 4 GiB wrapper
guard (observed around 4.33 GiB); the equivalent control module without
Glyphs compiled. AST parsing itself stayed small. The hot path was LLVM SROA:
stage1 represented large struct-return values as typed LLVM aggregate loads
followed by stores into hidden `sret` pointers. For `Glyphs.cover_blank`, SROA
expanded the copy of a 16 KiB `Coverage` value into 16,388 instructions,
after which `EarlyCSE` spent excessive memory processing the expanded body.
This was a backend representation/optimization pathology, not expected
front-end memory demand.

#### Source change and safety boundaries

In `worktrees/elisa-compiler-nw/src/backend/codegen_expr_construct.elisa`,
`emit_struct_construct_into_slot` recursively initializes an exact-type struct
literal directly in caller-provided storage. It prevalidates field positions
before evaluation, uses tri-state outcomes so unsupported expressions may
fall back only before emitting IR, applies explicit fields and omitted-field
defaults to their individual slots, and recursively avoids materializing
nested struct literals as aggregate SSA values. The return emitter uses this
path only for non-error functions returning an `sret` struct with no pending
`ensure` contracts; functions whose contracts observe `result`, error ABI
returns, non-exact types, and unsupported expression forms retain the ordinary
value path. Once any field initializer has emitted IR, the helper declines
instead of evaluating it a second time through fallback.

Earlier in this same candidate series, large safe zero values were changed to
target-sized `llvm.memset` operations. That path is restricted to
pointer-free integer/unsigned/bool/float scalar trees and arrays/structs made
only from those values; pointer-bearing aggregates continue to use the exact
LLVM null-constant semantics. These changes do not alter the wrapper's 4 GiB
limit, compiler optimization level, or oracle coverage.

The regression is now explicit in `nw-core/scripts/stage1_glyphs_memory_smoke.sh`:
it compiles the import-only Glyphs repro at both `-O1` and `-O2` using the
ordinary stage1 wrapper limit. `nw-core/scripts/gate.sh` invokes that smoke so
an import-only optimizer blow-up is caught independently of the larger native
game sweep.

#### Candidate identity and evidence

- Isolated artifact: `nw-core/build/elisac-stage1-wasm32-fixes-v12`, SHA-256
  `a7a9810f578533aacd7acac03470f972e5e42a575ec2a2c1a93a150bcd6f00c4`.
- Stage1 source fingerprint at seed/test time:
  `ee7f8bf59c5e560cd7b0eb78e75159c98f5a80c8d347152239368505f57db795`.
- Seed compiler: pinned stage0 at
  `nw-core/toolchain/elisac-stage0`, SHA-256
  `c5efa8ce20f781f21817eabc0481efe79a2c895031f49ce64bbb72911386c183`.
- Runtime object: `nw-core/toolchain/elisacore_runtime.o`, SHA-256
  `d392af4d754340af0b22ed7a00f9db8e66efbc0ab9dac034ac5c30d1f819b663`.
- Pinned stage1 remains SHA-256
  `e104009499aa46bd13859efb069eeea9240266f05f2bd09bd76017925fa5d4f3`;
  pinned binaries and `nw-core/toolchain/PROVENANCE` were not modified.
- The import-only Glyphs `-O2 -emit llvm` compile completed through the normal
  memory-guard wrapper in 0.29 seconds, with maximum RSS 79,724,544 bytes

- The emitted O0 `Glyphs.cover_blank` and `Glyphs.templates_blank` bodies

### 2026-09-14 — readonly-reference owner resolution and concurrency-decline scope

This entry supersedes the COMP-006 and concurrency-decline status in the
earlier snapshot only. It is focused compiler-source evidence; it does not
close the compiler gate or any application/game milestone.

#### COMP-006 implementation and verification

The readonly checker in
`worktrees/elisa-compiler-nw/src/semantic/check_readonly_ref.elisa` now records
the owning module for every function signature and resolves direct calls
before consulting mutable-reference parameter contracts. It distinguishes
module-local, top-level, uniquely visible imported, and explicitly qualified
one-segment calls. By-value declarations are represented too, so a local
same-name function cannot accidentally inherit another module's mutable-ref
contract. The ordinary readonly-argument and immutable-struct-field
address-of checks share this owner resolution. The expanded test covers
positive and negative cases, overload exemptions, qualified calls, and
visibility isolation. Its imported-call case seeds semantic visibility
metadata directly, and nested module paths/aliases remain unverified.

#### Exact scope of the 21 body declines

The v12 stage1 WASM warning names the following bodies in
`elisacore_std/elisacore_runtime_concurrency.elisa`: `mutex`,
`mutex_dispose`, `mutex_lock`, `mutex_unlock`, `condvar`, `condvar_dispose`,
`cond_wait`, `notify_one`, `notify_all`, `yield_thread`, `sleep_usec`,
`ctx_concurrency_join_handle`, `spawn_raw`, `detach_raw`, `ctx_pool_lock`,
`ctx_pool_unlock`, `ctx_pool_wait`, `ctx_pool_signal`, `ctx_pool_broadcast`,
`ctx_pool_state_new`, and `pool_shutdown`. The audit found no calls/imports for
these symbols in `nw-core/src`, `nw-core/shells`, or `nw-core/test`, and no
matching imports in that v12 WASM module. They are therefore classified as an
unexercised runtime surface for the current app, not as fixed, implemented, or
generally safe. A future app dependency on one must add a call-site reproducer
and a real body/behavior check. The fresh v13 WASM artifact was rebuilt and
passed the artifact-level suite; its 17 imports also contain none of the 21
declined names. This does not implement those bodies, and later logs must
continue to report the warning.

### 2026-09-14 — Stage0 wide-comparison fix and default WASM rebuild

#### Root cause isolated

- The Marble controller increments its board-generation value after a tray
  transition, guarded by `run.board_generation < 9223372036854775806`. The
  field is mutable `i64`; on wasm32 the default `int` is only 32 bits. Stage0
  analyzed the unsuffixed comparison literal without taking the opposite
  field's integral type as context. Its emitted LLVM was
  `icmp slt i64 %board_generation, -2`: low 32-bit truncation of the positive
  literal followed by sign extension. With the runtime value at 1, the guard
  went false and the fallback reset generation to 1. Trial, rung, phase, and
  RNG seed were independently correct. Direct dispatch of the next-tray
  action reproduced it, excluding feedback timer scheduling.
- The first reduced fixture used a host target and therefore did not reproduce:
  64-bit host `int` can represent the limit. The permanent compiler parity
  fixture explicitly targets `wasm32-unknown-wasi`, contains a module-owned
  mutable `i64` field, and asserts the full positive constant in emitted IR.

#### Compiler correction

- Stage0 source in
  `worktrees/elisa-core-nw/compiler/src/semantic/analyzer_expr_operators_analyzebinaryexpr_to_analyzeenumispayloadpattern.go`
  now analyzes an unsuffixed integer value expression against the opposite
  integral operand for equality and ordered numeric comparisons. The helper
  recognizes an integer literal, parentheses around it, and unary minus;
  explicit numeric suffixes keep their existing type. `analyzeValueExpr`
  retains the existing fit validation for narrow integer types.
- Added `TestAnalyzeContextualWideIntegerComparisonLiteral` and
  `worktrees/elisa-compiler-nw/test/repro/contextual_wide_i64_comparison.elisa`
  with the parity driver
  `worktrees/elisa-compiler-nw/test/parity/contextual_wide_i64_comparison_smoke.sh`.
  Registered the smoke in `nw-core/scripts/gate.sh`. Before the source fix the
  wasm32 smoke failed on stage0's emitted `-2`; after it both stage0 candidate
  and current stage1 candidate emit `9223372036854775806`.
- Isolated stage0 candidate
  `nw-core/build/elisac-stage0-contextual-i64` has SHA-256
  `f976501a0e8d2f39a9bc1ac721ff13b6f95109ffbb90a7a557f6b0f91f8a1544` and was
  built from stage0 source fingerprint
  `00fbde8a5e92b6b11471a379eead635f9b98050d02bfc189d41b4912fc58c0f7`.
  The stage0 semantic regression and the wasm32 stage0/stage1 parity smoke
  pass. This is focused coverage, not a green full compiler gate.

#### Artifact promotion and verification

- Rebuilt the ordinary default artifact via
  `ELISACORE_BIN=build/elisac-stage0-contextual-i64 bash scripts/build_wasm.sh`.
  The resulting `nw-core/build/nwcore.wasm` is 406,315 bytes, SHA-256
  `223b0ea90cb57ccaeaeb9d05c0d1aa7f2d472afa5c235537971ea4d44a0b8847`.
  It includes the Count and Marble common-v1 task exports, so the current

#### Toolchain identity and compiler fixes

- Stage0 source HEAD is `5284109ca5805560a488c3b0a5d8cd4a1a45e317` and current
  source fingerprint is
  `3c7994cc3cdb7c2afecee335d13bcde0478532e62fddb1aef2000b8e53f2a43c`.
  The isolated Stage0 bootstrap candidate
  `nw-core/build/elisac-stage0-store-diagnostic` has SHA-256
  `26c88ad430a02b5171d50032762c7024d908b61b76b9910213ff3565efc6703b`.
- Stage1 source HEAD is `df6cf8172cf75cf7fe861c9591d7d03f16a0d7c6` and its
  exact current working-tree fingerprint is
  `2fa156c5c83e0f46e79e5676397345c91b0e650b00a5ce08018b1a3ec62ff5ca`.
  The upstream `origin/main` is still `fd2cb3cff470319500db362e5fce2833cbe300de`
  (the docs-only delta described above); the compiled working tree also contains
  its existing uncommitted compiler optimizations and fixes. Candidate
  `nw-core/build/elisac-stage1-current-source-20260914` has SHA-256
  `b78d2406c31794e11e9ea75e56ff106f682825aa6ffa071a9b0aeee58d645980`.
- The seed exposed a real Stage1-source/compiler-compatibility bug: inside
  `extend Parser`, `parse_machine_from_terminator` declared its result as the
  qualified `Parser.MachineFromTermAst`, which Stage0 resolved to `<invalid>`.
  Its caller's typed rebind correctly expected the aggregate, so code generation
  tried to store a `void` LLVM call result and LLVM aborted. The signature now
  uses the locally scoped `MachineFromTermAst`. A complete Stage1 `-O2` seed
  then succeeded.
- Stage0 code generation now diagnoses an LLVM `void` value passed to `storeValue`
  before calling `LLVMBuildStore`, and the declaration/reference-store error
  paths add function/local/source-line context. The check is deliberately limited
  to `void`; opaque-pointer reference stores may validly carry a different
  semantic storage type, so a broad semantic-type/LLVM-type equality assertion
  must not be added here.
- `nw-core/scripts/build_stage1_wasm.sh` now changes to its own `nw-core` root
  before invoking artifact tests. That makes the suite independent of the
  caller's current directory and fixes the `sessionapp_diff` import failure
  observed when the script was first launched from the repository parent.

### 2026-09-15 — Marble semantic ABI and collision-matrix checkpoint

This entry supersedes older Marble notes above wherever they describe the
trajectory count, context-loss status, or board-decoder coverage. It records
the state after the latest source-faithful renderer and lifecycle work; it is
still an implementation checkpoint, not a claim that the whole port plan is
complete.

#### Board transport boundary

`decodeMarbleBoard()` now treats the board bytes as an authenticated versioned
contract rather than as a sequence of convenient reads. The parser rejects an
invalid `built` or hole-home boolean encoding, a truncated fixed or variable
section, an oversized count before entering its loop, a non-finite float, an
out-of-range rung or dimensions, an inconsistent `width/depth = cell *
cols/rows + 2 * BOARD_MARGIN` relationship, a wall with reversed or
out-of-bounds extents, a non-positive geometry value, a hole outside the tray,
anything other than one final home cup matching the fixed home fields, a start
outside the usable tray, and trailing bytes after the declared payload. The
checks happen before a decoded board is handed to the renderer or physics
adapter. The explicit capacity tests remain separate from these semantic
tests, so a future ABI change must update both the parser and its resource
budget evidence.

`test/marble_board_abi_test.mjs` now exercises every one of those malformed
classes and then decodes all 16 generated rungs. The generated f32 boards still
pass, including the highest certified board and the maximum observed wall
count. The source/reference and isolated Stage0/latest-Stage1 comparisons
remain 80/80 deep-equal cases; this hardening change is host-side and does not
silently replace the production WASM artifact.

#### Native/WASM trajectory coverage

`test/marble_trajectory_reference_diff.mjs` now compares 33 scenarios and
1,632 per-frame states against Python 3.13.12/native MuJoCo 3.12.0 and the
official browser MuJoCo 3.12.0 package. The added cases explicitly verify that
a falling marble still collides with an explicit ball pair, and that an
already-lost marble remains terminal and parked while another marble continues
moving. The full measured maxima and assertion tolerances are unchanged; all
discrete states, event signals, counts, and continuous fields still pass.
The manifest now reports the corrected 33/1,632 totals and removes the stale
collision-mask wording from the remaining caveat. Uncovered work is still the
broader simultaneous-contact/corner and real play-session matrix, not an
unreported failure in the exercised cases.

#### Lifecycle status

The forced `WEBGL_lose_context` test and the active Marble-task integration
both passed live in headed Chromium. The shell observed a lost context, kept a
recovery token, installed a different renderer after restoration, reapplied the
active board, resumed the tray, and cleared the token with zero console errors
and warnings. The asynchronous texture callback and stale pre-loss WebGL
handle cleanup are guarded as well. Therefore context-loss/recovery is closed
for the measured renderer/task lifecycle; the remaining lifecycle caveat is
allocator behavior under other workloads and browser-tab shutdown. The 100
cycle `Escape -> Enter -> Space` memory repeat remains at a constant
10,223,616-byte WASM buffer with exactly 100 create/delete deltas and one
expected live model/data pair at the final tray.

The browser now preserves a test-gated per-trial ledger as well as the
aggregate summary. Each record contains the controller generation/trial/rung,
the source-derived board seed, physics elapsed seconds, common-controller
elapsed milliseconds, effective budget, home/lost/total-marble counts, the
native-style verdict, timeout flag, source `score()` win flag, and the par
time used for the report. The ledger is reset only when a new run is started or
destroyed, not when a feedback frame is redrawn; the generation guard prevents
duplicate records when several animation frames observe the same feedback.

A headed browser run with `{rung:2, trials:2, adaptive:true, seconds:15}`

### 2026-09-15 — Fresh headed Marble success replay

This checkpoint closes the first positive end-to-end Marble acceptance path in
the browser. Earlier live evidence proved that the shell could start a tray,
time it out, preserve the source scoring quirk, adapt from rung 2 to rung 1,
release held input on focus loss, recover from WebGL context loss, and clean up
MuJoCo resources. That was intentionally not treated as proof that a player
could actually reach the home cup through the browser shell. The following
replay supplies that missing positive result.

#### Exact setup

1. Serve `nw-core` through `scripts/serve_web.sh`; do not use the `file://`
   URL because Firefox blocks the module/WASM fetch and the shell must show an
   actionable transport error instead of an indefinite loading screen.
2. Open the test-gated URL
   `http://127.0.0.1:8000/shells/web/index.html?marble-seed=17&marble-test-hooks=1`.
3. Set the persisted Marble options to:
   - starting rung `1`;
   - one trial;
   - adaptive difficulty `false`;
   - shadows `false` for this input/physics acceptance pass;
   - explicit tray budget `45` seconds.
4. Navigate through the real controls: `Games`, category `Attention`, task
   `Marble Maze`, then Space to enter and Space to start.
5. Confirm that the first board is the deterministic seed `889418965` and
   that the status identifies the official MuJoCo WASM path.

The route used below is deliberately recorded in two alphabets. The native
trajectory test calls the physics adapter directly with tray directions. The
source UI maps keyboard controls to tray directions as follows:

| Native tray direction | Source UI key | Browser route position |
| --- | --- | --- |
| W (west) | A / ArrowLeft | 1, 10 |
| S (south) | S / ArrowDown | 2, 3, 11, 12 |
| E (east) | D / ArrowRight | 4, 5, 6 |
| N (north) | W / ArrowUp | 7, 8, 9 |

Therefore the exact held keyboard route is `A, S, S, D, D, D, W, W, W, A,
S, S`. Each key is held for 300 ms, released, followed by a source-compatible
`L` level command, and followed by 600 ms of coast. The level command matters:
the native reference route calls `Simulation.level()` after every direction

### 2026-09-16 — source-score semantics, latest compiler rebuild, and browser proof

The previous Marble implementation had a semantic split at the exact place
where the original source is intentionally surprising. The source physics
verdict answers one question: did every marble reach the home cup before the
tray deadline? The source `score()` method answers a different question: did
the result row contain zero lost marbles? Therefore a tray can time out with
no marble lost, display a physical timeout/loss verdict, and still contribute
one win to the aggregate score. Treating only the physical all-home result as
the controller win silently changed the original scoring behavior.

The fix is deliberately explicit rather than hidden in the web ledger:

1. `MarbleMazeGame.Run` now tracks `score_recorded` separately from the
   physical `verdict`.
2. `ACTION_REPORT` accepts a two-bit result value. Bit 0 is the physical
   all-home verdict; bit 1 is the source score win derived from the physics
   lost count. The controller rejects an impossible bit pattern in which the
   physical verdict is all-home but the score bit is clear.
3. A timeout finalizes the physical controller state first and leaves the
   score commit to the host, because only the MuJoCo adapter owns the
   authoritative lost-marble count at that boundary.
4. `ACTION_SCORE=10` commits one source-score result during feedback. It is
   accepted only once for the active board and is ignored after the result has
   already been recorded. This keeps retries idempotent and prevents a
   renderer or repeated animation frame from inflating the aggregate.
5. The browser sends the one-shot score action immediately after observing
   feedback, reads `marbleGame.lost`, and then records the same result in the
   presentation ledger. The stable twelve-field common state envelope did not
   change; only the Marble semantic action/report contract was extended.
6. The runtime protocol validator now allows action code 10 and validates the
   report bitmask, score payload, and auxiliary-field boundaries before the
   controller sees them.

The regression sequence now covers all of the boundary cases that can expose
the old bug: an invalid report bitmask is rejected; a valid all-home report
sets both bits and increments the win; a timeout enters feedback with a
physical loss; an explicit zero-lost timeout score commit increments wins; a
nonzero-lost timeout commit increments losses; a duplicate report/score commit
does not increment either counter; and the final done state preserves the
source-shaped aggregate. The browser artifact suite passes this protocol smoke
alongside the complete task and Marble tests.

### 2026-09-16 — settle-frame clock synchronization

The Marble browser loop has two clocks by design: MuJoCo advances the physical
simulation first, while the common WASM controller receives the same active
frame delta afterward. That ordering is correct for timeout precedence—the
source checks whether the simulation settled before it checks the deadline—but
it creates a one-frame observation gap when the marble reaches home during the
current physics bite. Before this correction, `ACTION_REPORT` used the
controller's previous integer millisecond value for adaptive promotion and
public elapsed state, while the source used the just-completed
`Simulation.elapsed` value. Most runs differ by less than one frame and pass a
coarse result comparison; the discrepancy is still real at the exact `1.6 ×
par` adaptive boundary and could promote or fail to promote the wrong rung.

The fix is intentionally narrow:

- `MarbleMazeGame.ACTION_SYNC_SETTLE_TIME=11` is a host-only action. It is
  accepted only while the board is RUNNING, only with `aux=0`, only within the
  global duration bound, and only when the supplied value is not behind the
  controller's current elapsed value.
- On a physics settlement, the browser rounds the source simulation's elapsed
  seconds to milliseconds and dispatches this synchronization action before
  the existing two-bit `ACTION_REPORT`. It does not call the ordinary active
  clock advance on that frame, so a settlement exactly at the deadline still
  follows the source's settle-before-timeout precedence.
- `ACTION_REPORT` still carries `par_ms` in `aux`, so existing report callers
  and the stable state schema remain compatible. The new action changes neither
  the twelve fields nor their byte offsets; it only corrects the authoritative
  elapsed input before grading/adaptation.
- A rejected synchronization is logged as a controller diagnostic rather than
  silently reporting a success against stale time. The runtime validator
  rejects nonzero auxiliary data and the regression reuses the same event
  sequence after a deliberately malformed attempt to prove bad input does not
  consume ordering.

The focused ABI regression creates a Marble run, advances its controller to
`1000 ms`, rejects a malformed synchronization, accepts `SYNC_SETTLE_TIME` at
`1250 ms`, verifies the public state, and then accepts a physical win report.
The complete latest-compiler artifact suite and the isolated Stage0 suite both
pass after the change. The Stage0/latest-Stage1 board/MJCF oracle remains exact
for all 80 rung/seed cases, and the 36-scenario/1,932-state native/browser
physics differential remains green.

- product SHA-256
  `82543b75bb15bafd4e7a12aab824446b565f661a89a9870b34513c5722f34fc7`;
- active/served 873,782-byte WASM SHA-256
  `0c3b19b0fcefd4e497d00e3046fe48c8eec17466ea1cfae5eaa9a62a7f7510bc`;

### 2026-09-16 — transactional browser result ledger for Marble Maze

The browser shell now has a versioned, transactional result ledger in
`nw-core/shells/web/result-store.js`. The storage key is
`neural-workshop.results.v1`; records are validated before they are committed,
and malformed imports, duplicate record IDs, unsupported versions, unavailable
storage, and storage exceptions are rejected without claiming that data was
saved. A successful upsert replaces the record with the same session ID rather
than appending a second copy, which makes the write safe to retry after a
redraw, reload, or interrupted UI action.

Marble Maze creates one durable record when a run reaches DONE. The record
contains the session ID, task ID, creation/update timestamps, the effective
Marble options, completed/won/lost counts, best rung, and the complete ordered
per-trial result rows. The active controller remains separate from this
durable projection: persistence is attempted only after a new completed row is
recorded, and the UI reports `saved` or `unavailable` explicitly. This keeps a
storage-denied/private browsing mode honest instead of presenting an in-memory
run as a saved result.

The shell now exposes `Export results` and `Import results` controls. Export
serializes the validated ledger as JSON for backup/portability. Import parses
and validates the complete payload before merging it into the existing ledger;
an invalid import leaves the previous value untouched. The opt-in Marble test
hook exposes copied persisted Marble records for deterministic browser
assertions without exposing the storage implementation to normal task code.

Focused verification passed:

1. `node nw-core/test/result_store_test.mjs` covers upsert replacement,
   import merge, export round-trip, malformed-import atomicity, and denied
   storage.
2. `node nw-core/test/marble_renderer_contract_test.mjs` verifies the shell
   imports the ledger, renders the import/export controls, and wires completed
   Marble rows to the persistence path.
3. A headed Chromium run through Games → Attention → Marble Maze used the
   current optimized artifact, `rung=1`, one trial, adaptive off, a 15-second
   test budget, and seed `17`. The real run reached DONE after the timeout with
   one completed row, one score win, zero lost marbles, and
   `persistence="saved"`.
4. The persisted record ID was
   `marble-fa0d1727-8028-4588-b527-a363e3431150`; after a full page reload,
   the ledger still contained exactly that one record. The browser storage
   payload was 567 bytes, and the post-reload check reported no duplicate.

This closes the browser-side durable write, retry/upsert, and JSON backup path
for Marble results. It is deliberately not marked as complete APP-005 or
MM-004: native atomic-file writes, profile selection, date/statistics
aggregation, progress graphs, all-game adapters, full multi-option replay,
interrupted native-write recovery, and source-versus-port result differentials
remain open. The current browser ledger is the foundation for those later
adapters, not a substitute for them.

### 2026-09-16 — Concentration controller and browser integration implemented

This checkpoint implements the first complete common-v1 Concentration slice
described by the plan. It is an implementation checkpoint, not a claim that
the entire 45-game port is complete. Future agents must preserve the
authoritative-ownership and source-parity boundaries below when extending the
task.

#### Source contract and authoritative ownership

The source task is split across:

- `nw-core/src/tasks/concentration.elisa`, which owns deterministic board
  rules, CPython-compatible shuffle/deal, pair identity, `flip`, `peek_over`,
  `resolve`, `check_finished`, `hiding`, `cleared`, and source verdict values.
- `nw-core/src/scene_concentration.elisa`, which owns the reference card layout,
  text/image card projection, title/status/verdict text, and display-list
  command ordering.
- `nw-core/src/tasks/concentration_game.elisa`, which is the ABI-lifetime
  adapter and the sole authoritative owner of cross-call run state.

The controller must remain the only place that owns phase, deadlines, turns,
lapses, matched state, cursor, and verdict for the common WASM route. The
browser shell may retain only a handle, timer ID, and presentation caches. It
must never reconstruct the answer table, decide whether a pair matched, count
lapses, or infer DONE from a canvas frame. This separation is especially
important because the source lapse rule is identity-aware: seeing one physical
card of a pair is not interchangeable with seeing another physical card from
that pair.

#### Fixed-storage adapter design

`ConcentrationGame::Run` keeps the following state across ABI calls:

1. A mutable MT19937 stream, copied by value so each deal consumes the same
   persistent sequence as the source run.
2. Validated options: pair count, medium, peek duration, mismatch-hide
   duration, show-turns flag, and coach flag.
3. Fixed arrays for all 128 possible card slots: pair index, face-up flag, and
   matched flag.
4. Two flipped-card slots and 64 identity-set entries (`seen_a`/`seen_b`).
5. Phase, flipped count, turns, lapses, owed/deferred resolution flag,
   verdict, cursor, peek deadline, mismatch-hide deadline, start timestamp, and
   finish timestamp.

Every source-kernel operation follows the same lifetime protocol:

1. Validate the handle and operation at the common adapter boundary.
2. Reconstruct a temporary `Concentration::Board` from fixed arrays.
3. Copy all board fields into the temporary object, including identity sets;
   copying only visible cards or counters is incorrect.
4. Invoke the source kernel (`reset`, `deal`, `flip`, `peek_over`, or
   `resolve`) without duplicating its rule logic in the browser.
5. Copy every authoritative field back to fixed arrays/scalars.
6. Release the temporary source representation before returning from the ABI
   call.

No returned darray, pointer, or source arena allocation may be retained in
`Run`. If a future optimization changes the source Board layout, update the
copy-in/copy-out field list and add a regression that exercises identity
scoring, not merely a successful visual deal.

#### Options and stable ABI

The stable task ID is the unsigned FNV-1a hash of `concentration`,
`1179922742`. The six common create slots are:

| Slot | Meaning | Accepted values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `a` | pair count | `4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 30, 36, 42, 50` |
| `b` | medium | picture `0`, sound `1` |
| `c` | initial peek duration | `0, 500, 1000, 2000, 3000, 5000` ms |
| `d` | mismatch-hide duration | `300, 500, 700, 900, 1200, 1600, 2000` ms |
| `e` | show turn count | `0` or `1` |
| `f` | coach feedback | `0` or `1` |

The browser currently uses `(8, 0, 0, 900, 1, 0)` and seed `17`. The default
is deliberately a zero-peek picture route so browser smoke tests can start
directly in PLAYING while still exercising the same source deal. The focused
controller smoke separately covers a nonzero picture peek and sound mode.
Invalid pair counts, media values, durations, or booleans must return
`ERR_BAD_OPTIONS` before allocation or mutation.

#### Action, time, and pointer semantics

The controller action enum is deliberately minimal:

- `START=0` is accepted only in READY or DONE. It clears the prior run,
  redraws from the retained MT19937 stream, resets counters, and records the
  new start timestamp.
- `SELECT=1` carries a zero-based card slot in `value`. It is accepted only
  in PLAYING, for an in-range card that is not face-up and not matched.
  Selecting the second card starts the configured mismatch-hide deadline.

Space and Enter map to `START` in READY/DONE. A primary pointer-down is
translated from the common millionths coordinate range into the 912×684
reference viewport and then through `Concentration::layout_board` and
`Concentration::card_at`. The pointer conversion uses the same top/bottom
clearance bands as the scene; do not replace it with a guessed CSS grid.
Out-of-board clicks, secondary buttons, clicks during PEEK, clicks on matched
cards, and clicks on already face-up cards are ordered but ignored.

`advance(handle, logical_time_ms, elapsed_active_ms, sequence)` is the only
deadline transition path. At or after `peek_until_ms`, it calls
`Concentration::peek_over`. When two unmatched cards remain face-up and
`logical_time_ms >= hide_until_ms`, it calls `Concentration::resolve`. The
browser schedules one timer for the currently published deadline, rechecks
the phase/deadline after wake-up, and cancels the timer on task replacement,
exit, replay, or destruction. A stale timer must never advance a newly
created handle.

#### State and test accessors

The common 112-byte state frame exposes these twelve Concentration fields in
order: phase, pair count, card count, medium, turns, lapses, flipped count,
matched-pair count, verdict, cursor, show-turns flag, and coach flag. Phases
are `READY=0`, `PEEK=1`, `PLAYING=2`, and `DONE=3`; verdict is `-1` until
completion, then `1` for zero lapses or `0` for one or more lapses.

`nw_api_v1_concentration_info(handle, field)` exposes fields 0–15 in this
order: phase, pair count, card count, medium, turns, lapses, flipped count,
matched pairs, verdict, cursor, show-turns, coach, peek deadline, hide
deadline, started-at timestamp, and finished-at timestamp. The card accessor
uses field 0 for pair identity, field 1 for face-up, and field 2 for matched;
invalid fields or slots return the controller's documented negative sentinel.
These accessors are for deterministic tests and host rendering diagnostics;
they must not become a second mutable game API.

#### Scene and media strategy

The controller renders through `SceneConcentration::render`, passing a card
projection with stable image asset IDs `1000 + pair index`, source dimensions
64×64, face-up/matched flags, medium, turns, and phase/verdict messages. The
browser currently installs 64 generated, self-contained 64×64 canvas assets
as a temporary fallback source-media pool. This guarantees that a face-up
card is visibly distinct and that the render path has no network dependency;
it does not establish original-media parity. Before marking Concentration
visually complete, replace this fallback with the original asset catalog,
verify each asset's crop and dimensions, and keep the asset ID mapping stable
so native and browser scenes can share fixtures.

Rendering is observational. It must not advance a timer, consume MT19937,
resolve a pair, write persistence, or change a verdict. Future visual parity
tests must compare command ordering, card centers, font/text content,
matched-card treatment, sound-mode projection, and all viewport aspect ratios
against the original scene.

#### Browser integration sequence

The web route is wired in the following order:

1. `wasm_exports.elisa` includes the source kernel, scene, and controller and
   exports task ID/support, common lifecycle functions, Concentration info,
   and Concentration card accessors.
2. `runtime_protocol.elisa` validates options, sizes/initializes the fixed
   run, dispatches actions and pointer selection, advances deadlines, writes
   the common state frame, renders the scene, and destroys the run.
3. `index.html` requires the new exports, maps the task catalog's

### 2026-09-16 — Seen It Before? controller, ABI, and browser integration

This checkpoint implements the next source-backed vertical slice from GAME-008.
It is intentionally recorded after the Concentration checkpoint above because
the Recognition task exercises a different class of boundary: a planned stream
of fresh and repeated media identities, a delayed picture-concealment phase,
optional feedback, and a score that must distinguish four answer outcomes.
It does not close the entire 45-game port or API-001.

#### Source contract and the media boundary

The frozen reference for this slice is:

- `original-neural-workshop-enhanced/neural_workshop/ui/recognition.py`
  (`Recognition`), which owns option loading, the trial planner, phase
  transitions, answer handling, replay, feedback timing, scoring, and the
  picture/sound presentation policy.
- `original-neural-workshop-enhanced/neural_workshop/media.py`
  (`MediaPool`), which owns dataset filesystem paths, shuffle order, fresh
  allocation, and decoded pyglet objects.
- `nw-core/src/scene_recognition.elisa`, which owns title/status/footer
  placement, stage geometry, picture/sound projection, verdict placement, and
  Seen/New button geometry.

The source `MediaPool` cannot cross the common WASM ABI: it contains paths,
filesystem state, and decoded pyglet media. The port therefore keeps the
semantic boundary explicit rather than pretending that a JavaScript fallback
is the reference dataset. `RecognitionGame::Run` owns stable synthetic item
identities and all old/new decisions. The browser maps identity `i` to asset
ID `2000 + i`, installing 500 deterministic 64×64 picture canvases. This is a
testable media projection, not original-media parity. The sound medium keeps
the source phase semantics and the scene's sound plate, but real audio effects
remain an open effects-protocol task.

#### Controller storage and source-shaped planning

`nw-core/src/tasks/recognition_game.elisa` uses fixed storage so no arena-backed
darray survives an ABI call:

1. `Run` retains the MT19937 stream, validated options, phase, index, timing,
   verdict, last-correct value, and fixed arrays of up to 500 trial item IDs,
   repeat flags, and choices.
2. `build_run` creates the source-sized fresh pool, applies the repository's
   CPython-compatible shuffle helper, and consumes the shuffled pool in the
   same end-pop order as `MediaPool.take_many`.
3. At each trial position it scans only fresh presentations whose position is
   at least `min_lag` old and whose identity has not already been repeated.
   The repeat coin is drawn even when no candidate is eligible, matching the
   source control flow. A chosen repeat is marked so it cannot be repeated a
   third time; otherwise the next fresh identity is allocated.
4. `present` enters SHOWING and records the presentation clock. Picture mode
   with a positive study duration stores a deadline; sound mode deliberately
   stores no concealment deadline.
5. `answer` accepts only SEEN or NEW during SHOWING/HIDDEN, evaluates the
   expected choice from the controller-owned repeat flag, advances the index,
   and either enters 350 ms FEEDBACK or presents the next item immediately
   when feedback is disabled.
6. `advance` performs only the two source-timed transitions: picture SHOWING
   to HIDDEN at `now >= deadline`, and FEEDBACK to the next item/DONE at
   `now >= deadline`.
7. `score_field` computes hits, misses, false alarms, correct rejections, and
   answered count from the controller arrays. It never reads browser labels or
   infers an answer from a rendered asset.

The controller currently uses integer half-up percentage rounding for its DONE
summary. The original Python expression uses Python's `round`; if a future
cross-language parity corpus proves a half-even tie observable at 0.5%, the
summary formatter must adopt an explicit source-compatible integer rule and
add a tie-case regression. The underlying four-way counts are already exact.

#### ABI additions

The unsigned FNV-1a task ID for `recognition` is `3372563504`. The six create
slots are deliberately fixed and documented in `nw-core/docs/runtime-protocol.md`:

| Slot | Meaning | Accepted values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `a` | items per run | `10,20,30,40,60,80,100,150,200,300,500` |
| `b` | medium | picture `0`, sound `1` |
| `c` | repeat percentage | `20,30,40,50` |
| `d` | minimum repeat lag | `1,2,3,4,6,8,12,20,30,50,80` |
| `e` | picture study duration | `0,500,1000,1500,2000,3000` ms |
| `f` | per-answer feedback | `0` or `1` |

The common runtime additions are explicit branches in
`nw-core/src/wasm/runtime_protocol.elisa` for validation, allocation,
initialization, task info, action dispatch, key mapping, pointer-down mapping,
timed advance, common state serialization, rendering, support discovery, and
task ID. The additive exports in `wasm_exports.elisa` are:

- `nw_api_v1_task_recognition`
- `nw_api_v1_recognition_info`
- `nw_api_v1_recognition_item`

The common twelve-field state envelope is phase, total trials, index, medium,
repeat percentage, minimum lag, study duration, feedback flag, current item,
current repeat flag, last-correct flag, and deadline. The additive info fields

repeat, answered, and choice. `read_state` and `render` remain observational.

## 2026-09-16 — N-Cup Monte controller, browser route, and latest-compiler gate

This is the current handoff record for the N-Cup Monte slice. It supersedes
the older fourteen-controller checkpoint above without deleting that history.
The goal of this slice was to make the game a real source-backed lifecycle,
not merely replace the old “Game started” message with a new label. The
controller must remain authoritative for the hidden ball, the slot
permutation, the animation clock, the adaptive cup count, the result, and the
random stream. The browser may schedule callbacks and submit physical input,
but it may not infer or manufacture any of those facts.

### A. Reference contract that was audited before implementation

The source used for this slice is the frozen local reference at
`/Users/torarinvikbjarko/Documents/Coding Projects/Python Projects/neural-workshop-enhanced BACKUP`.
The relevant files are:

1. `neural_workshop/ui/ncupmonte.py`, which defines the presentation phases,
   source options, reveal/shuffle timing, smoothstep interpolation, slot
   geometry, pointer hit region, messages, and adaptive result behavior.
2. `nwenv/ncupmonte.py`, which defines the stepped task boundary: twenty
   possible ports, `choose_cup` as the only gameplay action, reveal/shuffle as
   clocked closed phases, and `start_round`/`deal` as the round-opening action.
3. `nw-core/src/tasks/ncupmonte.elisa`, the existing portable kernel, which
   defines the source table shape, CPython-compatible MT19937 calls, ball
   draw, cup permutation, pair sampling, and adaptive clamp.
4. `nw-core/src/scene_ncupmonte.elisa`, the existing display-list projection,
   which expects visual slots and identity labels separately and intentionally
   reveals the ball only in READY, REVEAL, and RESULT.

The exact source defaults are `start_cups=3`, `max_cups=8`, `adaptive=True`,
`swap_count=6`, `swap_ms=340`, `reveal_ms=1150`, and
`show_cup_numbers=True`. The six-slot common v1 options ABI has no slot for
the seventh number-display option, so the implementation fixes the source
default to true and exposes it as a read-only controller field. This is an
explicit compatibility decision, not an accidental browser default.

The source sequence is authoritative:

1. READY places cup identity `i` in visual slot `i` and waits for Space.
2. START draws one ball identity with `randbelow(cups)`, resets the identity
   permutation, enters REVEAL, and sets `deadline = now + reveal_ms`.
3. At the exact reveal deadline, the controller samples
   `max(1, swap_count + cups)` distinct slot pairs from the same persistent
   MT19937 stream. The swap plan is not generated early, because doing so
   would change the source random stream and could change the next deal.
4. Each planned pair runs for exactly `swap_ms`. Visual X values are
   interpolated with `t*t*(3-2*t)` after clamping elapsed time to the interval
   `[0, swap_ms]`. The identity permutation is exchanged only when the exact
   boundary is reached; the next pair begins at that same boundary timestamp.
5. After the last pair the controller enters GUESS. A pointer is hit-tested in
   the current visual coordinate system and returns the identity under the
   selected slot. A slot index must never be submitted as a cup identity.
6. CHOOSE records the guess and result, changes to RESULT, and adjusts cups by
   one only when adaptive mode is enabled. The result clamp is `[3, max_cups]`.
   The resulting current cup count is retained for the next START, matching
   the reference's `_place_cups()` behavior.

### B. Files and responsibilities delivered

`nw-core/src/tasks/ncupmonte_game.elisa` is the long-lived controller. Its
`Run` record contains only fixed-size ABI-safe data: persistent MT19937 state,
validated options, phase and score, deadlines, active swap indices, a fixed
20-entry identity permutation, a fixed 128-entry pair buffer, and fixed X,
start-X, and target-X arrays. The source `NCupMonte::Table` is constructed in
a temporary allocation region only for the deal and plan operations. Its
arrays are copied into the run before that region is destroyed.

The controller's public info fields are deliberately stable and numbered:

| Field range | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0..7` | phase, current cups, maximum cups, adaptive, configured swap count, swap duration, reveal duration, number-display flag |
| `8..11` | ball identity, guess identity, planned swap count, settled swap index |
| `12..16` | active deadline, active swap start, active elapsed, swap slot A, swap slot B |
| `17..20` | round number, hit count, miss count, last-correct flag |

The value fields are `ORDER=0`, `X=1`, `TARGET_X=2`, and `SWAP=3`.
`ORDER` is the cup identity in a visual slot; `X` is the current visual
coordinate; `TARGET_X` is the current pair's destination coordinate; and
`SWAP` is a pair-plan entry. Values outside the fixed range return `-1`.

`nw-core/src/wasm/runtime_protocol.elisa` adds:

- stable task ID `704181153`, the FNV-1a hash of `ncup_monte`;
- option validation for all six N-Cup fields;
- the N-Cup-specific `Run` allocation size;
- creation, info, action, advance, pointer, read-state, render, and destroy
  dispatch branches;
- `SPACE` and `ENTER` mapping to START in READY and RESULT;
- a pointer-down route that converts viewport millionths to the current cup
  identity before dispatching CHOOSE; and
- `nw_api_v1_ncup_monte_info` and `nw_api_v1_ncup_monte_value` adapters.

The allocation-size branch deserves explicit mention. During review, the
new task was initially inserted as the unconditional fallback in
`run_bytes()`. That meant Marble's valid create path allocated a N-Cup record
size and never reached its explicit Marble size. The artifact happened to
survive because the N-Cup record was larger, but that was an ABI ownership
bug. The branch now explicitly returns N-Cup size only for `TASK_NCUP_MONTE`
and returns the Marble size for the final Marble fallback. The full Marble
browser/physics/board/trajectory suite was rerun after this correction.

`nw-core/shells/web/index.html` adds the N-Cup route without duplicating
authority:

- the required-export guard includes the task ID and two accessors;
- `API_TASK.ncupMonte` points to the WASM task ID;
- the route creates `(3,8,1,6,340,1150)` with seed `17`;
- `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks call `apiAdvance` only while phase is
  REVEAL or SHUFFLE and stop automatically at GUESS/RESULT;
- Space/Enter start a round in READY/RESULT;
- pointer-down in GUESS is forwarded to the common pointer event path;
- task, category, screen, replay, and exit transitions cancel callbacks and
  destroy the old handle; and
- `window.__nw.ncupMonteInfo`, `ncupMonteValue`, `ncupMonteAction`,
  `ncupMonteFrame`, and `ncupMonteState` are read-only diagnostic helpers.

`nw-core/test/fixtures/task_catalog.json` registers N-Cup Monte as a
stateful-controller override with the kernel, scene, controller, exports, and
host capability map. `nw-core/scripts/test_wasm_artifact.sh` runs the focused
smoke as part of every artifact gate, so a fresh build cannot silently lose
the route while the generic 45-task catalog still passes.

### C. Animation and layout correctness checks

The controller originally recalculated all X positions on every render. That
would have erased a mid-swap interpolation on every browser animation frame,
making the final state correct but the actual cognitive task impossible to
follow. The layout now tracks both `layout_width` and `layout_cups` and returns
without rewriting positions when neither changed. A viewport resize or an
adaptive cup-count change still recomputes the rest positions. The active
swap's `start_xs` and `target_xs` are never replaced by a same-size render.

This is intentionally different from resetting the identity permutation:
layout only changes coordinates; `order` remains the authoritative visual
identity mapping. At a settled swap, the controller exchanges `order[a]` and
`order[b]`, resets X values to the source slot positions, increments
`swap_at`, and starts the next pair. On the final settle it enters GUESS and
clears active-pair fields without revealing the ball in the scene.

The browser smoke used both a typed action and a real headed pointer click.
The pointer click was computed from the controller's final `ORDER`/`X` data
only for test targeting; production JavaScript sends the physical canvas
coordinates and the controller performs the conversion. The test also checks
that a pre-deadline callback is ignored, an exact deadline settles a phase,
and a midpoint callback reports a nonzero smoothstep interpolation.

### D. Focused test contract

`nw-core/test/ncupmonte_game_smoke.mjs` now verifies:

1. stable ID and support discovery;
2. each invalid option class, including unsupported start/max/swaps/duration
   values and a non-boolean adaptive flag;
3. the exact common 112-byte state envelope and READY values;
4. observationally stable READY rendering and the source title/message;
5. Space START versus typed START equivalence for the same seed;
6. source ball range, reveal deadline, and persistent round counter;
7. pre-deadline rejection and exact reveal-boundary transition;
8. `swap_count + cups = 9` planned pairs for the default three-cup round;
9. distinct active pair slots and a real midpoint smoothstep displacement;
10. all nine exact swap boundaries and final GUESS state;
11. visual-slot-to-cup-identity pointer selection;
12. correct scoring, hit count, result message, and adaptive promotion to four
    cups;
13. next-round persistence of the adapted cup count and RNG stream; and
14. idempotent handle destruction.

### B. Source options and lifecycle specification

The controller accepts exactly these source option sets:

| Field | Accepted values | Default used by the browser |
| --- | --- | --- |
| total targets | 10, 20, 30, 40, 60, 80, 120, 200, 300, 500 | 40 |
| base lifetime | 400, 600, 800, 1200, 1600, 2200, 3000, 4000 ms | 1600 |
| spawn gap | 150, 250, 400, 550, 700, 1000, 1500, 2000 ms | 700 |
| maximum active | 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12 | 3 |
| starting size | 60, 80, 100, 130, 170, 220, 280 px | 130 |
| adaptive | `0` or `1` | `1` |

The lifecycle is deliberately explicit:

1. Creation validates every option, seeds one persistent MT19937 state, clears
   all target and score storage, and returns READY.
2. START clears any prior run data, resets the lifetime to the configured
   base, records the logical start time, and enters RUNNING.
3. While RUNNING, `advance(now_ms)` expires every target whose source lifetime
   has elapsed, records misses, and spawns at most one target when the spawn
   deadline is due and both the total and active limits allow it.
4. A target receives an immutable sequential identity, normalized position,
   birth timestamp, target-specific lifetime, and deterministic asset ID. Its
   visible side shrinks as time advances; the target is gone at the exact
   source threshold, not one animation frame later.
5. A pointer event is converted to the source coordinate system and tested
   against current target rectangles. If rectangles overlap, the smallest
   current target wins. The controller removes the selected target by identity,
   records reaction time, updates hits/accuracy/mean, and applies the source
   adaptive success rule.
6. An expired target increments misses and applies the source adaptive miss
   rule. Empty clicks do not manufacture a miss or hit.
7. A new target clears the transient verdict before it becomes visible. Once
   all targets are spawned, DONE is entered only after the active list becomes
   empty. A result remains controller state and is not inferred from a label.

The fixed reference coordinate system is 912 × 684 logical pixels. X uses a
half-side margin. Y uses the source band boundary plus the half-side margin and
the source upper margin. The browser may scale this scene to CSS pixels, but it
must not resample the target or move target identity during a resize.

### C. Controller and ABI implementation

`nw-core/src/tasks/reflex_game.elisa` is the authoritative long-lived
controller. Its `Run` record contains:

- persistent MT19937 state;
- validated total/lifetime/gap/active-limit/size/adaptive options;
- phase, clock, spawn deadline, current lifetime, verdict, and reaction state;
- fixed arrays for twelve active target identities, positions, birth times,
  target lifetimes, and asset IDs; and
- a fixed five-hundred-entry reaction sample buffer for the largest supported
  run.

Arena-backed temporary values are not retained as pointers. Target fields are
copied into the fixed record before any temporary region can be released.
`remove_target` shifts all fields together, so identity, geometry, timestamp,
and asset cannot become misaligned after a hit or expiry. `expire_targets`
iterates without skipping the record shifted into the removed slot.

The task-specific info ABI is stable and documented in
`nw-core/docs/runtime-protocol.md`:

| Info fields | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0..8` | phase, total, spawned, max active, base lifetime, gap, start size, adaptive, current lifetime |
| `9..14` | hits, misses, presented, accuracy, mean reaction time, active count |
| `15..18` | verdict, logical clock, next spawn deadline, last reaction time |

The value ABI is:

| Value field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | target identity |
| `1` | normalized X |
| `2` | normalized Y |
| `3` | birth timestamp |
| `4` | target lifetime |
| `5` | remaining lifetime in parts per million |
| `6` | deterministic media asset ID |

Values outside the active/fixed ranges return the documented invalid-value
sentinel. Read-only accessors never allocate, mutate score, or advance time.

`nw-core/src/wasm/runtime_protocol.elisa` adds the Reflex branches in every
relevant dispatch point: options validation, `run_bytes`, creation, info,
action, valid-action checking, key mapping, pointer dispatch, logical advance,
common-state serialization, rendering, support discovery, task ID, and
destruction. Space and Enter map to START only in READY or DONE. The pointer
path accepts physical millionths and performs the source-coordinate conversion
inside the controller path; it does not accept a browser-selected target index.

`nw-core/src/wasm/wasm_exports.elisa` includes the kernel, scene, and
controller and exports the task ID plus Reflex info/value accessors. The
browser's required export list includes all three new symbols, so serving an
older WASM file fails explicitly instead of silently returning the old start
placeholder.

### D. Browser integration and ownership rules

`nw-core/shells/web/index.html` integrates Reflex through the real task hub:

- `API_TASK.reflex` is populated from `nw_api_v1_task_reflex()`;
- the browser default run is `(40,1600,700,3,130,1)` with seed `17`;
- `installReflexAssets()` currently installs deterministic numbered 64×64
  canvas tiles at IDs 3000–3063, preserving target identity while the
  original media pool is still open work;
- `ensureReflexRun()` creates the handle only for Games → Attention → Reflex;
- `taskStarted` sends START through the common action path;
- `requestAnimationFrame` calls `apiAdvance` while RUNNING and stops when the
  controller returns DONE;
- pointer-down forwards viewport coordinates to WASM; it never decides which
  target was clicked;
- task/category/screen/replay/exit transitions cancel the frame callback and
  destroy the old handle; and
- `window.__nw` exposes read-only Reflex diagnostics for tests without making
  those diagnostics part of production authority.

The browser's responsibilities are deliberately narrow: schedule a clock,
convert CSS coordinates, look up an asset ID, and draw commands. The browser
does not maintain a second target array, score, lifetime, verdict, random
generator, or adaptive level.

## 2026-09-16 — Moving Targets controller, browser route, and latest-compiler gate

This is the post-Reflex implementation record for GAME-011, the original
Moving Targets task. It is intentionally a handoff-quality ledger rather than
a claim that the task is source-identical or that the whole plan is finished.
The implementation replaces the former browser-side “Game started” response
with a source-backed controller whose random deal, ball motion, hidden target
identity, phase deadlines, pointer selection, score, adaptive target count,
and completion state live in WASM. The browser supplies a monotonic clock,
viewport coordinates, and display-list presentation only.

### A. Reference files and contract reconstructed before editing

The frozen reference checkout is:

`/Users/torarinvikbjarko/Documents/Coding Projects/Python Projects/neural-workshop-enhanced BACKUP`

The source contract was audited across the following layers:

1. `neural_workshop/ui/tracking.py` defines the visible task title and
   instructions, the ball scatter, target-count selection, source reference
   geometry, cue/tracking/picking/reveal deadlines, pointer behavior, verdict
   message, and the visible round counters.
2. `nwenv/tracking.py` defines the environment-level start and step boundary,
   the action vocabulary, and the timing semantics that the UI drives.
3. `nw-core/src/tasks/tracking.elisa` supplies the portable MT19937-backed
   `Tracking::deal_round` generator and `Tracking::bounced` movement helper.
   These helpers are used directly by the controller; the browser does not
   reimplement the random scatter or bounce equation.
4. `nw-core/src/scene_tracking.elisa` defines the existing source-shaped
   display-list projection for title, phase instructions, balls, target
   highlights, picked marks, counters, and verdict text.
5. Shared `Geometry`, `Verdict`, `Scene`, and display-list modules define the
   reference-coordinate conversion and command encoding used by the common
   WASM renderer.

The stable ID is `moving_targets = 228173702`, the unsigned 32-bit FNV-1a
hash of the stable string. The ID is returned by the Elisa runtime, recorded
in the catalog fixture, and obtained by the browser from
`nw_api_v1_task_tracking`; gameplay code does not hand-copy the numeric ID.

The source option domains are retained exactly for this slice:

| Slot | Meaning | Valid values | Browser default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `a` | ball count | 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 20, 25, 30 | 8 |
| `b` | requested tracked targets | 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15; clamped below ball count | 2 |
| `c` | tracking seconds | 3, 5, 8, 10, 15, 20, 30, 45, 60 | 8 |
| `d` | speed percent | 8, 12, 16, 22, 30, 40, 55, 75 | 16 |
| `e` | rounds | 3, 5, 8, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50 | 5 |
| `f` | adaptive target count | 0 or 1 | 1 |

The controller phases are explicit and ordered:

1. `READY` has no active round and accepts only START.
2. START resets score and adaptive state, deals round one, and enters
   `CUEING` for the fixed two-second source cue. Ball positions are static in
   this phase.
3. At the exact cue deadline the controller enters `TRACKING`; it does not
   advance the balls by the elapsed cue interval. Tracking movement begins
   with the next positive interval.
4. During `TRACKING`, every call to `advance(now_ms)` moves all balls with the
   source bounce helper. The controller caps a single integration interval at
   100 ms to keep a paused tab from tunneling through a wall. At the exact
   tracking deadline it stops movement and enters `PICKING`.
5. During `PICKING`, pointer coordinates are converted to the fixed 912×684
   reference scene and tested against each ball's current radius. A target is
   identified by its immutable spawn index, not by a browser list position.
   Clicking a ball toggles its picked flag; selecting all requested target
   identities scores the round immediately.
6. A scored round enters `REVEALING` for the fixed 1.8-second source reveal.
   Adaptive success increments the next target count after a perfect round;
   any missed target decrements it. Both are clamped to the source range and
   to `ball_count - 1`.
7. At the exact reveal deadline the next round is dealt, or the controller
   enters `DONE` after the configured number of rounds. Late `advance` calls
   against DONE are observational and cannot create another round.

The fixed reference geometry is 912×684. Ball radius is derived with the
shared height scale and source minimum. Scatter bounds include the source
fractional top and bottom margins and the 2.4-radius minimum separation. The
source generator's random draw order is preserved by calling
`Tracking::deal_round` once per round and copying its temporary flock into
fixed controller arrays before the generation region is destroyed. The
current implementation intentionally keeps the reference aspect ratio in the
controller; a future resize-parity packet must prove whether the Python UI's
actual aspect-dependent bounds need to become a host-supplied viewport option.

### B. Controller storage and ABI

`nw-core/src/tasks/tracking_game.elisa` owns a fixed `Run` record containing:

- one persistent MT19937 state;
- validated ball count, requested target count, seconds, speed percent,
  derived speed, round count, and adaptive flag;
- phase, current round, deadline, last tick, verdict, and all cumulative
  counters;
- fixed arrays of thirty X/Y positions, X/Y velocities, target flags, and
  picked flags; and
- no retained arena-backed slice or temporary `Tracking::Flock` pointer.

The task-specific info fields are stable `i64` fields `0..18`:

| Field | Meaning |
| ---: | --- |
| 0–6 | phase, balls, starting targets, seconds, speed percent, total rounds, adaptive |
| 7–9 | current tracked count, round number, active deadline |
| 10–16 | asked targets, picked count, caught targets, completed rounds, cumulative asked, cumulative caught, verdict |
| 17–18 | last controller tick and maximum tracked count |

The value fields `0..6` are read-only per-ball values: stable ball index,
normalized X, normalized Y, X velocity, Y velocity, hidden target flag, and
picked flag. Invalid indices and fields return the established negative
sentinel. Reading state, info, values, or rendering never consumes RNG,
advances time, selects a target, or changes score.

The common state envelope emitted by `nw_api_v1_read_state` is twelve `i64`
values in this order: phase, round, total rounds, balls, asked, tracked,
total caught, total asked, picked, caught, verdict, deadline. This is the
common envelope; callers that require source fields use the additive tracking
info/value accessors and must not infer hidden target identity from the scene.

`src/wasm/runtime_protocol.elisa` has Moving Targets branches in every
required lifecycle location: stable task constant, option validation,
allocation size, creation, task info, action dispatch, valid-action checking,
keyboard mapping, pointer dispatch, logical advance, common state encoding,
tracking info/value accessors, display-list rendering, support discovery,
task-ID lookup, and destruction. Space and Enter map to START only from READY
or DONE. Pointer input is accepted only from PICKING. The runtime does not
expose an action for directly changing a ball or declaring a target caught.

`src/wasm/wasm_exports.elisa` includes the tracking kernel, controller, and
scene and exports `nw_api_v1_task_tracking`,
`nw_api_v1_tracking_info`, and `nw_api_v1_tracking_value`. The browser's
required-export guard includes all three symbols, so an older WASM file fails
at load time instead of falling through to the former placeholder behavior.

### C. Browser integration and resource ownership

`shells/web/index.html` integrates the task through the real task hub path:

- `API_TASK.tracking` is read from the exported stable ID;
- Moving Targets is Attention-category index 2, after Reflex and N-Cup Monte;
- the browser defaults to `(8, 2, 8, 16, 5, 1)` with seed 17;
- `ensureMovingTargetsRun()` creates one common-v1 handle for the selected
  task and never allocates a parallel JavaScript ball model;
- task start sends the semantic START action through WASM;
- `requestAnimationFrame` advances only during CUEING, TRACKING, and
  REVEALING, and stops when the controller reaches PICKING, READY, or DONE;
- a pointer-down during PICKING forwards reference coordinates to WASM and
  then reschedules the reveal clock so the final pick cannot leave the browser
  frozen in REVEALING;
- task, category, screen, replay, and exit transitions cancel the frame
  callback and destroy the prior handle; and
- `window.__nw` exposes read-only Moving Targets diagnostics for regression
  tests, while production rendering remains driven by the display-list bytes.

The browser owns no target set, hidden answer, score, adaptive counter,

state.

## Current Lookout slice — 2026-09-16

Lookout is now the eighteenth source-backed common-v1 browser controller. This
section is the exact handoff packet for the implementation and its current
limits. It establishes a working, source-shaped controller and browser route;
it does not claim original-media parity, native/Python/SDL support, complete
options persistence, or closure of GAME-013.

### A. Reference contract and source audit

The frozen reference was audited in:

- `original-neural-workshop-enhanced/neural_workshop/ui/lookout.py`;
- `original-neural-workshop-enhanced/neural_workshop/configdefaults.py`;
- `original-neural-workshop-enhanced/neural_workshop/taskoptions.py`;
- the portable kernel `nw-core/src/tasks/lookout.elisa`; and
- the scene contract `nw-core/src/scene_lookout.elisa`.

The stable ID is `lookout`; its unsigned FNV-1a task ID is `3096915418`.
The source defaults are eight shapes, colour watching, 16-percent speed, a
2,000 ms morph gap, ten cues, and adaptive shape count. The exact option ABI is
`(shape_count, watching, speed_percent, morph_ms, cue_count, adaptive)`:

| Slot | Source domain | Meaning |
| ---: | --- | --- |
| `a` | `3,4,5,6,8,10,12,15,20,25,30` | starting shape count |
| `b` | `0,1,2` | colour, form, or both channels |
| `c` | `8,12,16,22,30,40,55,75` | drift speed percentage |
| `d` | `800,1200,2000,3000,5000,8000` | morph interval in milliseconds |
| `e` | `5,10,15,20,30,50` | cues per run |
| `f` | `0,1` | adaptive shape-count adjustment |

The reference has two independently scored signal channels. Colour is the `J`
answer and form is the `F` answer. When both are enabled, each channel has its
own seen timestamp and can independently become a hit or miss; the current
reference `answer` resolves the episode through the requested channel and its
feedback gate prevents another answer until the next cue. A cue is a colour/form
pair selected by shuffling all 24 candidates and taking the first minimum
coverage candidate. Every matching live channel is then morphed away before
the cue starts, so a new episode cannot begin with a free hit.

The source random stream and update order are part of the contract:

1. Lay out all positions before drawing any drifter's heading, pace, colour,
   form, or next-morph deadline.
2. If the spacing attempt budget is exhausted, relax separation in place; do
   not restart the layout or rewind the RNG.
3. Integrate drift with `dt` clamped to 100 ms, aspect-correct horizontal
   motion, and reflected bounds.
4. Process due morphs in array order. A normal morph changes colour with a
   70-percent branch or form otherwise and retries until the identity changes.
5. If a live channel has been dry for more than six seconds, force a matching
   colour or form on a randomly selected dry channel at the next morph.
6. Record a channel's first appearance timestamp. If it disappears after
   being seen, record a miss and return immediately, leaving the other channel
   for the next episode exactly as the reference does.
7. On a hit, record `now - seen_at` in the source reaction-time array before
   clearing seen markers for feedback. Adaptive hits add one shape and misses
   subtract one, clamped to 3..30.
8. Hold feedback for 1,400 ms, drift the flock during feedback, resize the
   flock at the source feedback boundary, then select the next absent cue or
   enter DONE at the configured cue count.

### B. Controller storage and temporary-region boundary

`nw-core/src/tasks/lookout_game.elisa` is the ABI adapter. The portable kernel
uses arena-backed `darray` values, so its `Lookout::Run` and `Lookout::Flock`
are materialized only inside a large temporary region for `start`, `advance`,
and `answer`. Before leaving the region, every durable value is copied into the
fixed controller record. No arena pointer is retained in a heap `Run` and no
source object crosses an export call boundary.

The fixed record contains:

- one persistent MT19937 state and the six validated source options;
- source and controller phase values (`READY`, `WATCHING`, `FEEDBACK`,
  `DONE`), cue number, cue colour/form, cue and feedback deadlines, and the
  monotonic controller clock;
- seen flags and timestamps for both channels;
- hits, misses, false alarms, reaction count, 256 reaction-time slots, verdict,
  feedback message kind/channel, and the last reaction in milliseconds; and
- thirty fixed X/Y positions, X/Y velocities, colours, forms, and next-morph
  timestamps.

The adapter intentionally distinguishes configured `start_count` from current
materialized `shape_count`: READY has no flock yet and reports zero live shapes;
after START, the live count equals the source count and changes only at source
feedback boundaries. The `answer` adapter captures `seen_at` before calling the
source `Lookout::answer`, because that source call clears the seen markers as
it enters feedback. This ordering is covered by the 150 ms reaction-time smoke
case and prevents a feedback transition from turning every reaction into a
zero or “now” timestamp.

### C. Common API and render contract

`runtime_protocol.elisa` has Lookout branches for stable ID lookup, option
validation, allocation size, create, task info, semantic action dispatch,
action-code validation, Space/Enter mapping, action payload validation,
advance, common-state encoding, task-specific accessors, display-list render,
support discovery, and destruction. The semantic actions are:

| Action | Value | Valid effect |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `START` | `0` | READY or DONE → start/replay |
| `COLOR` | `1` | answer the colour channel while WATCHING |
| `FORM` | `2` | answer the form channel while WATCHING |

Space and Enter map to START only from READY or DONE. Direct channel actions
are ignored outside WATCHING or when that channel is not live under the selected
watching mode. Invalid payloads do not consume event order.

The twelve common state fields are emitted in this order: phase, cue number,
total cues, live shape count, watching mode, hits, misses, false alarms,
reaction count, verdict, feedback-until timestamp, and controller clock. The
task-specific info fields `0..20` expose all source options, cue identity,
score, mean reaction, deadlines, last reaction, and current shape count. Value
fields `0..6` expose normalized X/Y, velocity, colour, form, and next-morph
timestamp for a valid shape slot. Read and render operations are observational:
they do not consume RNG, advance the clock, change score, or mutate the cue.

`SceneLookout` remains the sole projection. It renders the title, source status
line and cue number, live cue glyph, footer keys, flock glyphs, verdict, and
feedback text. It preserves the source's Okabe-Ito colour table, four-form glyph
family, reference 912×684 coordinate system, cue-glyph placement beside the
measured status line, and source draw ordering. The browser does not rebuild
glyphs from task-specific arrays or decide whether a cue is present.

### D. Browser ownership and route

The real route is Games → Attention → Lookout. It is selected at category index
2, task index 3. `shells/web/index.html` now:

- requires the Lookout task/info/value exports before accepting the WASM file;
- reads the task ID from the export rather than hard-coding it in production;
- creates one common-v1 handle with `(8,0,16,2000,10,1)` and deterministic seed
  17 for the default route;
- sends START through the common key/action path;
- schedules `requestAnimationFrame` only during WATCHING or FEEDBACK and passes
  the browser's monotonic elapsed timestamp to `advance`;
- maps `F` to FORM and `J` to COLOR, matching the source footer;
- ignores pointer clicks for this keyboard task rather than inventing a second
  hit-test authority;
- renders only the WASM display-list bytes and uses task-specific accessors for
  the status note and regression diagnostics; and
- cancels the frame callback and destroys the handle when the task, category,
  screen, options menu, or replay changes.

The browser owns only scheduling, keyboard translation, canvas presentation,
and the CSS/reference viewport. It does not own the flock, cue, random stream,
seen timestamps, score, reaction times, or adaptive count. `window.__nw` exposes
Lookout state/info/value helpers only for deterministic browser verification.
